## Gain Margin

Displays the gain margin of a complex analog waveform in decibels (dB). The gain margin is the difference between the gain of the measured waveform and 0 dB at the frequency where the phase shift is -180-degrees.

This measurement might fail if the phase of the measured waveform does not pass through -180-degrees or if the waveform is not complex.

## Phase Margin

Displays the phase margin of a complex analog waveform in degrees. The phase margin is the difference between the phase of the measured waveform and the reference degree at the unity gain frequency. The reference can be either -180-degrees or 0-degree.

This measurement might fail if the magnitude of the waveform does not pass through 0 dB or if the waveform is not complex.

The following parameters can be set for the Phase Margin measurement:

|   Parameter | Description                              |
|-------------|------------------------------------------|
|        -180 | Specifies the reference as -180 degrees. |
|           0 | Specifies the reference as 0 degrees.    |

## Dpu

Calculates the total number of defects per unit based on the points in a waveform. Given one or both of an upper and lower specification limit, the Dpu is calculated as the area under a normal distribution that falls outside the specification limits. The mean and standard deviation of the normal distribution are equal to the mean and standard deviation of the points in the waveform.

## Eye Measurement Methodology

The permanent default value for vref, vdc, and vac is 0.0. The vref, vdc, and vac values calculate the MH, ML, OH, OL, WH, and WL without checking which one is specified.

You can calculate MH and ML using the following method:

```
MH = (lower limit of the upper eye) - (vref+vdc) ML = (vref - vdc) - (upper limit of the lower eye) You can calculate OH and OL using the following method: OH = (upper limit of the upper eye) - (vref+vac) OL = (vref-vac) - (lower limit of the lower eye)
```

WH is the eye opening width at level (vref+vdc). WL is the eye opening width at level (vrefvdc).

## Measuring PAM-N

Select the PAM-N eye measurement in the Measure Type section of the Automatic Eye Measurement dialog of the GUI.

<!-- image -->

The PAM-N measurement measures a pulse amplitude modulated signal with N amplitude levels (0, 1, 2, ..., n-1). Currently, PAM3, PAM4, and PAM6 measurements are supported. PAM3 measurement measures a pulse amplitude modulated signal with three amplitude levels (0, 1, 2) and two eye opens- Bottom Eye and Top Eye. PAM4 measurement measures a pulse amplitude modulated signal with four amplitude levels (0, 1, 2, 3) and three eye opens- Bottom Eye, Mid Eye, and Top Eye. PAM6 measurement measures a pulse amplitude modulated signal with six amplitude levels (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and five eye opens- Eye 0, Eye 1, Eye 2, Eye 3, and Eye 4.

The following figure shows an example for PAM3 measurement:

<!-- image -->

The options available in the Automatic Eye Measurement dialog are as follows:

## Input Parameters:

The following measurements are supported for PAM-N:

- Number of Levels - specify the number of amplitude levels of the measured signal. Currently, measuring signals with 3, 4, and 6 levels are supported.
- Eye Open Measurements - for slicer level based receiver, eye height/width are important:
- Mid-point - time and voltage level of the eye center of each eye
- Skew - time differences between the individual eye centers and eye center (at maximum height) of the center eye
- Height - vertical opening of each eye open at certain y level, x value, or eye center

<!-- image -->

- Width - horizontal opening of each eye open at certain y level, x value or eye center
- Area - outline of the eye area that is calculated
- Level Measurements - for ADC based receiver, level variation in constellation form is most important
- Mean - amplitudes at specified x value, eye center or minimum thickness for each level
- Thickness:
- Peak-to-peak - Peak-to-peak values at specified x value, eye center, or minimum RMS for each level
- RMS - RMS values at specified x value, eye center, or minimum RMS from each level
- Skew - time differences at eye center or minimum thickness to the eye center of the center eye for each level
- RLM - Level separation mismatch ratio
- Amplitude Levels (VA,VB,VC,VD) :
- Even Spaced - voltage amplitude levels are even spaced. By default, amplitude levels are automatically detected assuming the levels are even spaced.
- Compressed - voltage amplitude for various levels are too high or too low. In this case, you must specify the amplitude levels.

## Timing Reference - reference values/measurements are based on:

- Based on Center Eye - time reference for all eye opens is based on eye center of center eye
- Each Eye Independently - time reference for each eye open is based on eye center of each eye itself
- Specify References - time reference for eye open is based on VREF specified. If required, Select X value to specify

## Eye Open Measurements Reference - reference values/measurements are based on:

- Calculate DVDT Min/Max/Avg - select to automatically measure the DVDT values for minimum, maximum, and average slew rates of PAM4 eyes. Default- Unselected
- Offset from Mid-Point - specify the offset from mid-point to calculate DVDT values of PAM4 eyes.

<!-- image -->

- Calculate Area - select to measure the area and display the outline of the area for each eye opening.
- Step Size for Accuracy (%) - specify the step size for accuracy to calculate the area of the eye diagram.
- Calculate Mask - select to specify the shape of the mask and reference X/Y values individually for each eye opening. The masks are shown for each eye opening.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

When setting up mask measurement, first specify the values for the bottom eye, then the middle eye, and then for the upper eye.

<!-- image -->

## Eye Center Location - determine the center of each eye:

- Maximum Eye Width - center of the eye is at the mid point of maximum width or width at specified y level
- Maximum Eye Height - center of the eye is at the mid point of maximum height or height at specified x value

Level Measurements Reference - determine the time/x value for level measurements:

- Eye Center - time of the level is the average of the centers of the adjacent eyes
- Minimum RMS - time of the level is at the minimum level RMS
- Time window used to determine the mean of the level and minimum RMS, percentage of UI

Measure Display - displays the results for eye open or level measurements based on selected measurements.

Measure Result - results tables for eye open/level measurements, with RLM result shown on the top of the Eye Level Measurements results table. This table extends by 9 rows for Open Eye Measurement if DVDT is calculated.

Apply to Selected Eye Panels - applies the measurement to all selected eye panels.

## Measuring Mask

The Mask measurement measures the best VREF for the specified mask where the largest vertical margin is found. The measurement returns the best VREF, the largest Vertical Margin, the UI time value, and the voltage value on the eye diagram where the largest Vertical Margin is found.

## Margins vs Mask Measurements

<!-- image -->

The following measurements are done in the Margins vs Mask section:

- Margins vs DQ and CA Diamond Mask
- Margins vs DQ Hexagonal Eye Mask

## Margins vs DQ and CA Diamond Mask

This measurement is done in the following manner:

- Y center is the VREF level of the maximum horizontal eye open, or the specified VREF level (using Set Mask VREF ).
- X center is:
- The mid-point of the width at the VREF level for a symmetrical diamond mask.
- The x location at the maximum vertical eye opening for an asymmetrical diamond mask.

The input mask configuration is as shown in the following image.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

You can load a specification file and use asymmetrical mask as shown in the following image.

<!-- image -->

## Margins vs DQ Hexagonal Eye Mask

This measurement is done in the following manner by training the Y and X positions to find the maximum summary of all the margin values of the six corners of the mask:

1. Find the maximum horizontal opening and VREF level.
2. Train the X position by placing the mask at the VREF level found earlier and move the mask along VREF horizontally to find the maximum sum of vertical margins.
3. Train the Y position by placing the mask at the X position found in step 2 and move the mask along the X position vertically to find the maximum sum of horizontal margins.

The input mask configuration is as shown in the following image.

## Using the Setup/Hold Results Viewer

To view the Setup/Hold Results Viewer:

1. Click the Detailed Results button in the Automatic Eye Measurement window.

The Setup/Hold Results Viewer window opens with the setup and hold results displayed.

<!-- image -->

2. Click one of the following display category types to display the results you want to see:
- Setup/Hold
- Setup+Hold
- Setup
- Hold

If you use a derate table, the margin, measured, and required values are reported, and the two corresponding rows that have the minimum setup and minimum hold margin are highlighted in yellow.

If you do not use a derate table, the minimum setup or hold times are reported, and the two corresponding rows that have the minimum setup or hold times are highlighted in yellow.

3. (Optional) Click the Data Slew Only check box to limit the display to data slew values only.

The worst slew values are reported at the bottom of the table. Exported results are also limited when this option is enabled.

4. (Optional) Click the Export button to export the selected results to a *.csv file.

## Creating ACE Scripts From DDR Measurements

To save an ACE script from the a DDR measurement you currently have set up, click the Script button in the Automatic Eye Measurement window.

For each DDR evaluation, the equivalent ACE TCL script is generated in the saved file in lines that are commented out. You can uncomment them to use these lines.

## Clearing Eye Measurements

Measurement results are displayed on top of the eye diagrams. Right-click an eye diagram, and choose Clear Measure from the menu that opens to clear the measure results.

## Copying Eye Diagram Settings

Eye diagram settings can be copied and reused on another eye diagrams. Right-click an eye diagram, choose Copy Settings from the menu that opens to copy the settings.

## Pasting Eye Diagram Settings

Copied eye diagram settings can be applied on top of another eye diagram by performing the following steps:

1. Open the eye diagram you want to apply the copied settings.
2. Right-click on the eye diagram, choose Paste Settings from the menu. The Copying Eye Configuration dialog opens.
3. Choose an eye configuration setting to apply.
4. Select the Measurement Settings check box to apply measurements settings along with the selected eye configuration setting.
5. Click OK.

## Measuring DDR3 Eye Diagrams

## Note:

A WaveView ADV license is required for this feature.

The following DDR3 Eye Diagram panel measurements are available:

- Derate-based setup and hold measurements
- tVAC measurements
- Ringback measurements

You can use these measurements during the design phase to create specifications from a behavioral model or for postsimulation verification.

## Measuring Derate-Based Setup and Hold Times

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Calculating Address, Command, Data Setup, and Hold Derating Values
- Setting Up DDR3 Measurements
- Viewing Derating Measurement Output

## Calculating Address, Command, Data Setup, and Hold Derating Values

The total setup time (tIS) and hold time (tIH) required is calculated by adding the base value of the setup and hold to the derating value. For example:

```
tIS Total= tIS(Base) + tIS tIH Total= tIH(Base) + tIH
```

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The base value of the setup or hold times is taken from the JEDEC standard. The following table shows sample setup or hold base values of several DDR3 specifications:

| Symbol          | Reference   |   DDR3-800 |   DDR3-1066 |   DDR3-1333 |   DDR3-1600 |   DDR3-1866 |   DDR3-2133 | Units   |
|-----------------|-------------|------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|---------|
| tIS(base) AC175 | V1HL(ac)    |        200 |         125 |          65 |          45 |             |             | ps      |
| tIS(base) AC150 | IH/L(ac)    |        350 |         275 |         190 |         170 |             |             | ps      |
| tIS(base) AC135 | VIH/L(ac)   |            |             |             |             |          65 |          60 | ps      |
| tIS(base) AC125 | VIH/L(ac)   |            |             |             |             |         150 |         135 | ps      |
| tIH(base) DC100 | V IH/L(dc)  |        275 |         200 |         140 |         120 |         100 |          95 | ps      |

The derating values of setup or hold times are calculated from the slew rate of the differential CLK and DQS signals, as well as the address, command, and data signals. In the JEDEC standard, the derating value lookup table corresponds to different slew rates of CLK or strobe and address, command, or data signals.

<!-- image -->

## Setting Up DDR3 Measurements

To set up a DDR3 measurement:

1. Load a 'derating table' by setting the following environment variable before invoking the WaveView tool:

```
setenv CX_DRTAB_FILE <derating_table_file>
```

This file contains the base values of setup andhold, as well aslookup tables for the derating valuesthat are from different DDR3 standards (DDR3-800/1066/ 1333/1600/1866/2133).

2. Launch the WaveView tool.

<!-- image -->

3. Plot the eye diagram for the address, command, ordata signal and specify the CLK/ DQS signal as the external trigger for the eye.

To create an eye diagram with external trigger, plot the eye diagram of the signal, then drag and drop the external trigger signal in to the lower-right corner of the eye diagram panel.

<!-- image -->

4. Ensure the blue triangle (trigger point) on the x-axis is at the center of the eye.
5. Right-click on the plotted eye diagram, and choose Measure Eye from the menu that opens.

The Automatic Eye Measurement window opens.

6. Specify theVref, DC, and AC values, and chooseaderatingtable from the Setup/ HoldDerating menu.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## 7. Click Measure .

The measurement is performed. Click Details to display the measurement report.

## Viewing Derating Measurement Output

Two kinds of measurement results are calculated:

- The required setup or hold values, which are calculated by adding the base value to the derating value. The derating values are obtained after measuring the slew values.
- The actual setup or hold values from the waveform.

If the actual measured value is less than the required value, then it is a setup or hold violation. The output report displays the slew values of signals, as well as the required and actual measured values of setup or hold.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

When you double-click a row, the measurements are displayed on a transient signal, which you can use for debugging the setup and hold violations. The transient portion of the signal that created the violation is displayed. The following figure shows the slew measurements and setup or hold measurements:

<!-- image -->

## Using the tVAC Measurement

tVAC is the required time above Vih (ac) or Vil (ac) for a valid transition. For a valid transition to occur, a signal has to remain above or below an AC threshold for a period of time. This time span is defined in the JEDEC standard. The tVAC constraint is slew-rate dependent similar to the setup or hold derating.

<!-- image -->

## Setting Up tVAC Measurements

The setup for a tVAC measurement is similar to setup or hold derating. To set up a tVAC measurement:

1. Before starting the WaveView tool, enter the following line to load a file that contains the value of tVAC:

```
setenv CX_DRTAB_FILE <tVAC_value_file>
```

The tVAC values can specify inside derating table file along with setup/hold derate values.

The measurement is performed after plotting the eye diagram with external trigger signal as in the case of setup or hold derating.

2. Open the WaveView tool.
3. Right-click the eye diagram, and choose Measure Eye from the menu that opens.

The Automatic Eye Measurement window opens.

<!-- image -->

4. Select atVAC table from the Setup/Hold Derate menu.
5. Click Measure .

The eye diagram is measured using the tVAC value.

<!-- image -->

## Viewing tVAC Measurement Output

If the measured tVACvalues are smaller than the required value, violations are flagged red in the report that is created after the tVAC measurement is performed.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

You can click on any of the rows in the report that shows the transient signal and tVAC measurement. In the following figure, the tVAC violations are displayed on a transient waveform:

<!-- image -->

## Measuring Ringback

The ringback measurement calculates how far the top side of a waveform dips below the AC threshold while not crossing the DC threshold. If the waveform moves below the DC threshold, then a ringback violation occurs.

118.8n

118 9n h1119. 031nle 1 2119.192n119 3n The ringback measurement setup is similar to the tVAC measurement setup in that you also need to provide a tVAC table. The ringback is measured when a signal goes above AC threshold and then goes below the AC threshold values.

<!-- image -->

## Viewing Ringback Measurement Output

Ringback results can occur with or without violations. The output report displays the ringback voltage value. A ringback value without a violation is a signal that goes above the AC threshold, then goes below AC threshold, and finally stays within the AC and DC thresholds. A ringback value with a violationis a signal that goes above the AC threshold and then goes below the DC threshold.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Ringback violations are highlighted in red in the report. When you select a row in the report, the ringback measurement is displayed on a transient signal. The following figure shows the ringback violation displayed on a transient signal in magenta:

<!-- image -->

## Measuring DDR4 Eye Diagrams

## Note:

A WaveView ADV license is required for this feature.

The following DDR4 measurements are supported in the WaveView tool:

- Vcent measurements from a Vref sweep
- Vcent\_Dq (pin avg)
- TdiVW
- VIHL\_AC
- TdiPW
- Tr&amp;Tf based on VdIVW\_Total
- SRIN\_dIVW based on VdIVW\_Total
- TdIVW &amp; VdIVW margins
- Aperture alignment for LPDDR4

Please refer the JEDEC Manual (JEDEC standard no 79-4) for the details of these measurements.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Taking DDR4 Measurements
- Taking TdIVW and VdIVW Margin Measurements
- Aligning the Aperture for LPDDR4 Measurements
- Shifting the Trigger Clock Delay and Delay Clock to the Aperture Center
- Sample DDR4 Specification File

## Taking DDR4 Measurements

This section explains how to take the following DDR4 measurements:

- Taking Vcent Measurements
- Taking TdIVW\_Total and VIHL\_AC Measurements
- Taking TdIPW, Tr, Tf, and SRIN\_diVW Measurements

<!-- image -->

## Taking Vcent Measurements

When a Vcent measurement is performed, the Vref value that corresponds to widest eye opening is calculated. If multiple eye diagrams exist on a single panel, the Vcent value of each eye is measured, and the average value is calcualted to get the Vcent\_DQ pin average.

To take a Vcent measurement:

1. Right-click the eye diagram, and choose Measure Eye from the menu that opens.

The Automatic Eye Measurement window opens.

2. Click the DDR4 measurement.
3. Click the Input Parameters tab.
4. Click the Enable check box to enable a Vref sweep.

The Vcent\_DQ pin average for all the bits is calculated when this option is enabled.

5. Enter an AC value (VdIVW\_Total/2), as well as the Start , Stop , and Step values.
6. Click the Measure button.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The values for Vcent are calculated and displayed in the Measure Result field, as well as on the eye diagram.

## Taking TdIVW\_Total and VIHL\_AC Measurements

To take TdIVW\_Total and VIHL\_AC measurements:

1. Right-click the eye diagram, and choose Measure Eye from the menu that opens.

The Automatic Eye Measurement window opens.

2. Click the DDR4 measurement.
3. Click the Input Parameters tab.
4. Enter values for Vref and AC , and click the Measure button.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The values for TdIVW\_Total and VIHL\_AC are calculated and displayed in the Measure Result field, as well as on the eye diagram.

If you want to specify a target value for TdIVW\_Total and VIHL\_AC in a DDR4 specification file and load it into the WaveView tool, enter the setenv CX\_DRTAB\_FILE &lt;filename&gt; environment variable at the command line before invoking the WaveView tool. See the Sample DDR4 Specification File section for information on how to set up a DDR4 specification file.

Include the following commands in your DDR4 specification file to set these values:

```
#min_aperture <value> or #min_aperture_ui <value> #min_vihl_ac <value>
```

If a measured value does not meet the target, the violations are highlighted in red.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Taking TdIPW, Tr, Tf, and SRIN\_diVW Measurements

To take TdIPW, Tr, Tf, and SRIN\_diVW measurements:

1. Right-click the eye diagram, and choose Measure Eye from the menu that opens.

The Automatic Eye Measurement window opens.

2. Click the DDR4 measurement.
3. Click the Input Parameters tab.
4. Enter values for Vref and AC , and click the Measure button.

The values for TdIPW, Tr, Tf, and SRIN\_diVW are calculated and displayed in the Measure Result field, as well as on the eye diagram.

5. Click the Detailed Results button.

ExDort xClose

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The Setup/Hold Result Viewer window opens with the TdIPW, Tr,Tf, and SRIN\_diVW values displayed. You can double-click a row to show the corresponding measurements on a transient signal.

If you want to specify the target value for the TdIPW and slew, you can include the following commands in your DDR4 specification file:

```
#min_dataslew <value> #min_tdipw_ui <value>
```

Measurements that do not meet the target value are highlighted.

## Specifying VIHL\_AC(min) for tr2 Measurements

You can specify the VIHL\_AC(min) value for calculating tr2 measurements:

1. Select DDR4 in the Automatic Eye Measurement window.
2. Check the VIHL\_AC(min) box and specify a value.

If a VIHLAC(min) value is not specified, by default the WaveView tool uses the calculated VIHL\_AC value.

If the specified VIHL\_AC(min) is too high or too low for certain clk period and tr2 cannot be calculated for that period, the Setup/Hold Result Viewer shows a horizontal line at y=VIHL\_AC(min).

## Taking TdIVW and VdIVW Margin Measurements

The following calculations occur when you place a mask inside of an eye and measure the voltage and timing margins:

- The Vcent value of each bit is calculated.
- The Vcent average of all the bits (Vcent\_Dq pin\_avg) is calculated.
- A mask based on the Vcent\_Dq and Triggering point is placed.
- The margin values are measured. The ringback effect is also considered during this measurement.

## To measure the margin:

1. Right-click the eye diagram, and choose Measure Eye from the menu that opens. The Automatic Eye Measurement window opens.
2. Click the DDR4 measurement.
3. Click the Input Parameters tab.
4. Click the Enable check box to enable a Vref sweep. The Vcent\_Dq pin average for all the bits is calculated when this option is enabled.
5. Enter the Start , Stop , and Step values. If you enter the Vref value directly, the measurement works without a Vref sweep.
6. Click the Report Margins vs Mask check box.
7. Choose a DDR4 spec from the DDR4 Spec menu that contains mask specifications.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Use the following commands in your DDR4 specification file to set the width and height of mask:

```
#mask_tdivw_ui <width value> #mask_vdivw <height value>
```

8. Click the Measure button.

<!-- image -->

Measiure Save Taraet XClose

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The mask margin is calculated and displayed in the Measure Result field, as well as on the eye diagram.

## Aligning the Aperture for LPDDR4 Measurements

Aperture alignment measures the mask offset values of each bit. You can plot the eye diagram of all the bits in a single panel and trigger it with a differential clock.

The first eye is used as the reference, and then the center point of the eye crossing is calculated. All other eye diagram center points are shifted so they overlap. Both the shift value of each bit and the aperture value are reported.

## To align apertures:

1. Plot the eye diagrams of all the bits in a single panel, and use the same signal for triggering the eye.
2. Right-click the eye diagram, and choose Measure Eye from the menu that opens. The Automatic Eye Measurement window opens.
3. Click the DDR4 measurement.
4. Click the Input Parameters tab, and enter Vref and AC values for the eye.
5. Click the Align Bit Apertures option.

## 6. Click the Measure button.

<!-- image -->

The shifted values of each bit are calculated and displayed in the Measure Result field.

## Shifting the Trigger Clock Delay and Delay Clock to the Aperture Center

Sometimes the simulation data might not have the trigger signal well centered, and you might want to center the trigger signal during the DDR4 measurement. The Trigger Clock Delay option specifies the delay value for the triggering signal, and the Delay Clock to Aperture Center option aligns the trigger signal to the center of the eye.

<!-- image -->

## RF Measurements

To open the RF Tool, choose RF Tool from the menu located in the Utilities section of the Waveform tab. The RF Tool window opens.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The RF Tool takes special measurements or calculations for RF analyses. The RF analyses in the RF Tool are different from the measurements in WaveView Measurement Tool-they are not applied to a specific signal, but to a specific waveform file.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Measuring Circles
- Measuring Noise Circles
- Measuring Stability Circles
- Measuring Operating Power Gain Circles
- Measuring Available Power Gain Circles
- Measuring VSWR Circles
- Exporting Equations From RF Tool Setup

## Measuring Circles

An S-Parameter waveform file is required for all circle measurements. The File selection field at the top of the RF Tool window lists all currently open waveform files. If the specified file is an S-Parameter waveform file, the frequency values are extracted from the specified file and listed in the Frequency List.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The center point and radius values for each circle are calculated. 360 data points are created to make a circle with the center and radius.

The result circles are plotted on a Smith Chart. If a Smith Chart does not yet exist in any waveview, a new one is created, and the circles are plotted on it.

This section contains information on the following topics:

## Measuring Noise Circles

To measure a noise circle in the RF Tool:

1. Click the Noise category on the left side of the RF Tool window.

The Noise Circle measurement settings are displayed.

2. Choose a file from the File menu that contains the noise circle you want to measure.
3. Enter a dB noise figure value in the Noise Figure text box, or click the Noise Figure Sweep check box if you want to include a noise figure sweep as part of the measurement.

## Note:

System Impedance value is not an input value, but is the value of signal Zo.Zo(1) or Zo.Zod(1) from the selected waveform file. The value is displayed for informational purposes.

4. Select one or more frequency values by holding the Ctrl key and clicking frequency values in the Frequency List.

If you want to select all frequency values, pres Ctrl + A to select all.

5. Click Apply to take the noise circle measurements and plot the results.

## Measuring Stability Circles

To measure a stability circle in the RF Tool:

1. Click the Stability category on the left side of the RF Tool window.

The stability circle measurement settings are displayed.

2. Choose which S Parameter signals you want to include as part of the measurement in the S Parameters section.

<!-- image -->

The associated signals and parameters are defaults from the selected waveform file. You can change the defaults signals by choosing different signals from the menus in the S Parameter section.

3. Select one or more frequency values by holding the Ctrl key and clicking frequency values in the Frequency List.

If you want to select all frequency values, pres Ctrl + A to select all.

4. Choose the type of stability circle you want to plot. You can choose one or both types.

Click the Output Stability Circle check box to plot an output stability circle waveform. Click the Input Stability Circle check box to plot an input stability circle waveform.

5. Click Apply to take the stability circle measurements and plot the results.

## Measuring Operating Power Gain Circles

To measure an operating power gain circle in the RF Tool:

1. Click the Operating Power Gain category on the left side of the RF Tool window.

The operating power gain circle measurement settings are displayed.

2. Choose which S Parameter signals you want to include as part of the measurement in the S Parameters section.

The associated signals and parameters are defaults from the selected waveform file. You can change the defaults signals by choosing different signals from the menus in the S Parameter section.

3. Choose one of the following gain values:
- Value

Enter a gain value in the Value text box.

- From/To Sweep

Enter from and to values in the From and To text boxes, respectively. Enter a Step value as well.

- Gmax-based Sweep

Enter step and number values in the Step and Number text boxes, respectively.

4. Select one or more frequency values by holding the Ctrl key and clicking frequency values in the Frequency List.

If you want to select all frequency values, pres Ctrl + A to select all.

5. Click Apply to take the operating power gain circle measurements and plot the results.

## Measuring Available Power Gain Circles

To measure an available power gain circle in the RF Tool:

1. Click the Available Power Gain category on the left side of the RF Tool window.

The available power gain circle measurement settings are displayed.

2. Choose which S Parameter signals you want to include as part of the measurement in the S Parameters section.

The associated signals and parameters are defaults from the selected waveform file. You can change the defaults signals by choosing different signals from the menus in the S Parameter section.

3. Choose one of the following gain values:
- Value

Enter a gain value in the Value text box.

- From/To Sweep

Enter from and to values in the From and To text boxes, respectively. Enter a Step value as well.

- Gmax-based Sweep

Enter step and number values in the Step and Number text boxes, respectively.

4. Select one or more frequency values by holding the Ctrl key and clicking frequency values in the Frequency List.

If you want to select all frequency values, pres Ctrl + A to select all.

5. Click Apply to take the available power gain circle measurements and plot the results.

## Measuring VSWR Circles

To measure a VSWR circle in the RF Tool:

1. Click the VSWR category on the left side of the RF Tool window.

The VSWR circle measurement settings are displayed.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Choose which S Parameter signals you want to include as part of the measurement in the S Parameters section.

The associated signals and parameters are defaults from the selected waveform file. You can change the defaults signals by choosing different signals from the menus in the S Parameter section.

3. Choose the type of VSWR circle you want to plot. You can choose one or both types.

Click the Output VSWR Circle check box to plot an output VSWR circle waveform, and enter a value for VSWROut. Click the Input VSWR Circle check box to plot an input VSWR circle waveform, and enter a value for VSWRIn.

4. Select one or more frequency values by holding the Ctrl key and clicking frequency values in the Frequency List.

If you want to select all frequency values, pres Ctrl + A to select all.

5. Click Apply to take the VSWR circle measurements and plot the results.

## Exporting Equations From RF Tool Setup

To export an equation of the setup from an RF measurement to the Equation Builder:

1. Ensure you set up all the necessary settings for an RF measurement.
2. Click the To Eqn button at the bottom of the RF Tool window.

The Equation Builder opens with the created RF measurement equation. For example, the following equation is exported from the settings for a noise circle measurement:

```
nc("0|gsmlna.sc0","50 60 10",50,"100M 200M 300M")
```

## PrimeSim HSPICE Measure Tool

To open the PrimeSim HSPICE Measure tool, choose HSPICE Measure from the menu located in the Utilities section of the Waveform tab.

## Pareto Analysis

The Pareto Analysis tool can import your data mining results from PrimeSim HSPICE, performs sensitivity, R, and R^2 calculations, then produces results in one of the following formats:

- HistBar plot
- scatter plot

- text window plot
- text file

To perform a Pareto analysis:

1. Choose Pareto Analysis from the menu located in the Utilities section of the Waveform tab.

The Pareto Analysis window opens.

<!-- image -->

2. Select an Input Signal by dragging it from the signal list and dropping it in the text box.

The input signal can be from an *.mt or *.mc file (which are files that contain parameter names and values for each trace you can load by clicking Browse ), or from a measurement you apply to a sweep tr0 signal. The number of points in this signal need to be equal to the number of sweeps. Signals are not editable.

3. Ensure a Param File is selected.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

You can click the Browse button to browse to the location of a Param File, or enter the name in the Param File text box.

4. Choose which parameter signals you want to include by clicking the check box next to a signal name listed in the Parameter Name table.

By default all signals are selected. You can deselect all signals by unchecking the check box in the heading row.

5. Choose one or more analysis types: Sensitivity , R^2 , or R .

## Using the Equation Builder

This chapter details using the Equation Builder in the WaveView tool.

equation b ld r p g The Equation Builder facilitates multi-file mixed-signal waveform operations and measurement. You can create and evaluate equations on waveform files to generate results as scalar measurements or new waveform data.

You can type input equations into the Equation Builder or construct them by dragging and dropping from the Waveform signal browser or from the WaveView tool. You can evaluate any or all equations at once, each on one or more specified target waveform files.

The following sections describe the Equation Builder:

- Viewing the Equation Builder
- Adding an Equation
- Building an Equation
- Setting the Target File of an Equation
- Evaluating Equations
- Plotting Results
- Marking Annotation Information From Equation Results
- Setting Up Macros
- Saving DDR Equations as ACE Scripts
- Calculating Multi-trace Waveforms

<!-- image -->

## Viewing the Equation Builder

Click Equation Builder in the Utilities section of the Waveform tab to open the Equation Builder. The following window appears.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Viewing the Equation Builder Keypad

When an equation is selected, the black Close button toggles the following equation keypad window to add or edit expressions to the equation.

Disabled areas of the image were explained on the previous page.

<!-- image -->

## Using the Text Editor

The equation builder text editing behaves as follows:

- Bracket and quote completion: When typing a left bracket or left quote, the tool completes the right side automatically.
- Function completion: When typing, the tool matches the input with existing functions and display them in a pop-up form as follows:

<!-- image -->

Press Tab to select the first function in the pop-up list, press Esc to close the pop-up list, and use the preference Hide function completion for calculator to disable this feature.

- Function selection: You can quickly select an entire function and signal in the equation string with a single click, which highlights it as follows:

<!-- image -->

Interaction with a highlighted function is as follows:

- Typing anything replaces the entire highlighted string.
- Dragging a signal onto the highlighted string replaces the entire string.
- Clicking again on the highlighted string (or double-clicking) changes to type-in mode.
- Clicking the white space outside of the function will enter type-in mode and place the cursor at the end of the string.

## Adding an Equation

To add a new equation, click Input new equation here in the equation list. You can then type or use the equation keypad to build an equation, as detailed in Building an Equation.

## Building an Equation

## Adding Signals to an Equation

To add a signal to an equation, drag and drop the signal from the Waveform Browser or WaveView, or right-click the signal in the Waveform Browser and select Signal "Name" &gt; Add to Equation from the context menu.

When dragging and dropping, you can drag the signal into an equation in the equation list, or into a Signal text field within the equation keypad.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

You can also type a signal name directly into an equation in the equation list. In this case, note that to add a signal using case-sensitive name search, you should use the wave() function to access the signal. For example:

```
wave('I(Vdd)')
```

If the target file for an equation has not been set, adding a signal automatically populates the Target column with the related waveform file.

## Adding Multiple Signals From Different Waveform Files to an Equation

When using multiple signals from different waveform files in a single equation, you need to specify the index for each signal after the first so that it corresponds to the correct waveform file.

To add these waveforms and assign the correct index:

1. Add each signal to the equation as shown in Adding Signals to an Equation.

You see that multiple waveform files are automatically populated in the Target column for that equation:

<!-- image -->

The index number for each signal corresponds to the order of the waveform files in the Target list, as shown above.

2. Format the signals with the corresponding index in the format of:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

Please note that the first (top) waveform file always has an index of 0 and does not need to be specified; this means that the second file has a file\_index of 1, the third file has a file\_index of 2, and so on.

See Changing the Index Number of a Target File to change index assignments.

## Adding Functions to an Equation

To add a function to an equation from the equation keypad:

1. Click the Functions tab and select a function from one of the subtabs.

The right side of the keypad displays information for adding that function.

2. Add a signal to the function as shown in Adding Signals to an Equation.
3. Enter information for any needed options and click Add .

You can also type a function directly into an equation in the equation list.

See Supported Functions for a list of all functions supported by the Equation Builder.

The following sections detail additional function options:

- Viewing Function Arguments
- Function Nesting
- Adding User-Defined Functions
- Adding User-Favorite Functions

## Viewing Function Arguments

When a function is selected, the function dialog shows the arguments of the current function. To change an argument within the function, make changes in the text fields and select Update . For example:

<!-- image -->

## Function Nesting

When a function is selected and highlighted as described above, double-clicking a function in the function list of the keypad nests the currently highlighted string. Behavior changes depending on the number of arguments in the function, as follows:

- If the function has one argument, the function nests the current string and the new function is highlighted.
- If the function has more than one argument, the current string is set as the first argument and the cursor is placed into the line editor of the second argument.

## Adding User-Defined Functions

You can define user functions through the GUI by clicking Define User Function in the Equation Builder window.

Once user-defined functions are loaded, they are displayed in the User category and the appropriate category based on return value ( Meas or Wfm ). This User category replaces the previous Macro category, and contains both macros and TCL functions. If there are no macros or TCL functions, the User category is hidden.

## Adding User-Favorite Functions

To add a function to your favorites, right-click the function from one of the common categories and select Add to favorites . To remove a function from your favorites, rightclick the function in the Favorites category and select Remove from favorites . If there are no user-favorites, the Favorites category is hidden.

To add a .MEASURE statement to an equation from the equation keypad:

1. Click the Measures tab.

The .MEASURE options are displayed.

2. Enter information for any needed .MEASURE options and click Add .

See the HSPICE Reference Manual: Commands and Control Options for further information on the .MEASURE statement.

## Naming an Equation

Once an equation has been named with an alias, it can be referred to by this alias in subsequent operations.

To name an equation, either click the cell under the Name column for that equation and type a name, or assign a name in the equation itself with a prefix.

For example, entering the following equation will name the equation as POWER :

```
POWER='I(VDD)'*'VDD"
```

To rename an equation, repeat the above or select Signal "Name" &gt; Edit Alias from the Waveform Browser context menu and enter a new name for it.

## Setting the Target File of an Equation

For each equation, you can select the target file in the Target column. If you dragged the signal from the Waveform Browser or the WaveView tool, the target file is set automatically.

## Changing the Target File of an Equation

You can change the target of an equation to any imported waveform file.

To change the target file of an equation:

1. In the equation list, click the dropdown arrow in the Target column.

A dropdown menu appears with a list of all imported waveform files:

<!-- image -->

2. Click a file to set it as the target of the equation.

## Changing the Index Number of a Target File

If there are multiple target files used in a single equation, each target file is assigned an index number. Each index number applies only to that equation.

To reassign the index number of a target file:

1. Highlight one or more equations in the equation list, then right-click and select Change Target Files from the menu:
2. In the Change Targets dialog, click No Change for the index number you want to reassign.:

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

A box appears listing all imported waveform files.

3. Select the target file to be assigned with the index number and click OK .

See Adding Multiple Signals From Different Waveform Files to an Equation for more information on when these index numbers are used.

<!-- image -->

## Evaluating Equations

To evaluate an equation, click its green Calculate button to the right in the equation list. You can use this to evaluate an equation as you build it.

To evaluate multiple equations at once:

1. In the equation list, check the box of each equation to evaluate:

<!-- image -->

You can also right-click an equation in the equation list and select Eval Current Equation with Sub-Equations to evaluate the entire equation as well as its subequations. Any evaluated subequations are added to the equation list.

## Evaluating Sub-Equations

To evaluate a single subequation, highlight the part of the equation you want to evaluate, right-click and select Eval Selected Equation . This will evaluate the highlighted subequation and add it to the equation list.

To evaluate all subequations, highlight the part of the equation you want to evaluate, rightclick and select Eval Selected Equation with Sub Equations . This will evaluate the selected equation and add it as well as every contained subequation to the equation list.

If the selected equation has no subequations, these options are disabled.

## Plotting Results

Once you have evaluated one or more equations, the results appear by default as follows:

- Scalar result (single or multiple scalars) - plotted to TableView.
- Waveform result - plotted to WaveView.

<!-- image -->

## Plotting All Results to TableView

To have all results plotted by default to TableView:

1. In the calculator keypad, click the ... button.

This brings up Operators | Units | Constants | Controls information.

2. In Waveform Results , check the Plot to TableView by Default box.

This preference is saved to the file when quitting WaveView.

## Plotting Selective Signals to WaveView

To plot all source signals in an equation, right-click an equation in the equation list and select Plot Signals in Current Equation .

To plot all source signals in a selected subequation, highlight part of an equation in the equation list, right-click, and select Plot Signals in Selected Equation .

To plot a single source signal, highlight a signal in an equation in the equation list rightclick, and select Plot .

## Marking Annotation Information From Equation Results

If there is annotation information, you can left-click the link in the Results column or rightclick and select Show in WaveView . For sweep scalar results, first expand the details. For example:

<!-- image -->

The annotation information contains lines, markers, and labels, with the following behavior:

- The line and markers are not movable. The labels can be dragged. All are fixed to the panel in which the signal was drawn.
- Deleting the panel/line deletes the annotation information as well.
- Moving the panel/line moves the annotation information as well.
- Copying the line or panel/line does not copy the annotation information.
- Annotation information is supported when saving/loading sessions.

<!-- image -->

## Setting Up Macros

Macros are available to repeatedly take measurements with created equations.

To set up a macro from the Equation Builder:

1. Click the Setup Macro button.

The Setup Macro dialog box is displayed.

2. Click Input macro definition here and enter the definition for the macro.

Macro definitions with an arbitrary number of input arguments are supported. For example:

```
FNEW(a,b) = a*b - 2 PI=3.1415
```

3. Enter a name in the Name (Args) column for the macro.
4. Press Enter .

Macro definitions can be imported or exported by clicking the Load and Save buttons.

<!-- image -->

## Saving DDR Equations as ACE Scripts

To save an ACE script for DDR-related equations you currently have set up, click the Save button in the Equation Builder window. Saved results can be restored using the Load button, or clicking Run ACE in the Script section of the File tab.

For each DDR evaluation, both the sx\_equation command and the equivalent ACE TCL script are generated in the saved file in lines that are commented out. You can uncomment them to use these lines.

## Calculating Multi-trace Waveforms

The Equation Builder supports operations on multi-trace sweep waveform data. Multi-trace waveforms are generated from parametric sweep analysis. An individual trace in a multitrace waveform is usually associated with a set of parameters.

When applying an equation to a multi-trace waveform, the equation builder operation is automatically repeated to every trace. As a result, multiple waveforms are generated from the operation.

For scalar measurement, a new measure-versus-trace signal is generated. The parametric() function can then be applied to the new measure-versus-trace signal to plot the measure result versus a selected parameter. For example:

```
AVG=mean('I(VDD') parametric(AVG,TEMP) or parametric(mean('I(VDD)',TEMP)
```

<!-- image -->

## Differences Between PrimeWave Expression Syntax and Standalone WaveView Expression Syntax

When using the PrimeWave Calculator or the WaveView Equation Builder, the tools assist you in creating expressions with the correct syntax. If you enter expressions manually, note that there are two main syntax differences between these tools.

## Signal name Syntax

- Standalone WaveView displays signal names as they appear in the waveform file. When referencing a signal name in a function, enclose the signal name in single quotes. If you use the Expression Builder to create an expression, single quotes are automatically added when you click the Add button.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## For example:

The current signal in waveform file is: P18:1

Using single quotes to wrap the signal name in a function: avgdev('P18:1')

A voltage signal name: v(rfout)

In a function avgdev: avgdev('v(rfout)')

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

- PrimeWave uses schematic signal names. The signal contains '/' before node names. When using the signal in a function, enter it directly, or click Pick From Schematic to select the nodes from the schematic.

<!-- image -->

For example:

A current signal name:

i(/P18/PLUS)

In a function avgdev:

avgdev(i(/P18/PLUS))

A voltage signal name:

v(/rfout)

In a function avgdev:

avgdev(v(/rfout))

- There is one exception in PrimeWave functions: signal()

In the PrimeWave Calculator function field, click Pick from waveform viewer , and select a waveform from WaveView. The signal is added with the signal() function.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The function retrieves a signal from a waveform file. Use the waveform file signal name syntax, but omit quotation marks when specifying the signal name. For more information, see signal.

For example, add a waveform P18:1 from WaveView to PrimeWave Calculator function avgdev :

<!-- image -->

## Add Signals From Different Waveform Files

- Standalone WaveView uses index numbers to add signals from different waveform files.

<!-- image -->

The first equation in the preceding image uses the signals from two files.

File D1/tran.tran is assigned to index 0.

File D2/tran.tran is assigned to index 1.

Create an avgdev equation, and select the signal P18:1 from D1/tran.tran .

Then add '+' with a second avgdev function. This time select P8:1 from D2/tran.tran .

The final equation is: avgdev('P18:1')+avgdev('1|P18:1')

The index of P18:1 is omitted because it is 0.

The second equation in the image uses the signals P18:1 and P8:1 from the same D2/tran.tran file. In this case, the file index can be omitted in the entire equation.

Summary of Standalone WaveView syntax with file index number:

- ◦
- Syntax: 'file\_index|signal\_name' file\_index and signal\_name pair are separated by |, and wrapped by single

quotes.

When file index is 0, the index can be omitted.

When all signals in one equation are from the same file, the index can be omitted.

For more information, refer to Adding Multiple Signals From Different Waveform Files to an Equation in WaveView User Guide .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Differences Between PrimeWave Expression Syntax and Standalone WaveView Expression Syntax

- PrimeWave uses the signal() function to add signals from different waveform files.

Invoke WaveView from PrimeWave and click Configuration &gt; Show/Hide Browser to show the WaveForm Browser.

Then open two files: D1:tran.tran and D3:tran.tran

Plot P18:1 from D1:tran.tran and P8:1 from D3:tran.tran .

<!-- image -->

In the PrimeWave Calculator function avgdev field, click Pick from waveform viewer .

Select P18:1 waveform from WaveView.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

In the Expression editing filed, append '+' after the first avgdev() function, then add the second avgdev() function. This time select the P8:1 waveform from WaveView.

The final expression is as shown in the following image.

<!-- image -->

There are other PrimeWave data functions that can specify the arguments of result type, analysis name, result directory and result file. They are in the category of Data Access Functions. Expressions with these functions can also specify signals from different results. For more information, see .

## Supported Operators

The following table summarizes the supported operators.

| Operator/Function   | Alias   | Description             |
|---------------------|---------|-------------------------|
| +                   |         | Addition operator       |
| -                   |         | Subtraction operator    |
| *                   |         | Multiplication operator |
| /                   |         | Division operator       |
| ^                   | **      | Power operator          |
| ?                   |         | Ternary operator        |
| %                   |         | Integer operator        |

Mathematic functions can operate on scalars or waveforms. The returned value can be a scalar (or a waveform) if its input argument is a scalar (or signal).

## Supported Constants

The following table summarizes the supported constants.

| Constant Name          | Variable Name   |            Value |
|------------------------|-----------------|------------------|
| Pi ( )                 | c_pi            | 3.14159265358979 |
| 2*Pi                   | c_2pi           | 6.28318530717959 |
| Elementary Charge (qe) | c_qe            |   1.60217662e-19 |
| Euler's number ( )     | c_e             | 2.71828182845905 |
| K                      | c_k             |     1.380649e-23 |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Constant Name   | Variable Name   |            Value |
|-----------------|-----------------|------------------|
| sqrt(2)         | c_sqrt2         | 1.41421356237310 |

## Supported Logic Operations

The following table summarizes the supported logic operations.

| Operator   | Logic Function   | Notes            |
|------------|------------------|------------------|
| &          | AND              | Bitwise or unary |
| &#124;     | OR               | Bitwise or unary |
| ^          | XOR              | Bitwise or unary |
| ~          | NOT              | Bitwise only     |
| >>         | SHIFT right      |                  |
| <<         | SHIFT left       |                  |
| ~&         | NAND             | Unary or binary  |
| ~&#124;    | NOR              | Unary or binary  |
| ~^         | XNOR             | Unary or binary  |

## Note:

You can add the 'b 'o 'd or 'h prefix to a logic operator to specify binary, octal, decimal, or hexadecimal, respectively. For example:

```
6'b010=6'b000010 9'o077=9'b0001111111 4'd010=4'b1010 12'h0F0=12'b000011110000
```

## abs

Measures the absolute value of a given signal or value.

## Syntax

abs(&lt;signal&gt;,[&lt;type&gt;])

## Returns

A signal or scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;

The signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

## &lt;type&gt;

(Optional) Specifies to perform the function in a discrete or continuous way. Default value is discrete.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found

## Examples

```
abs('0|v(out)') abs(-5)=5 abs($sig,'discrete') performs abs in a discrete way. abs($sig,'continuous') perform abs in a continuous way.
```

## acos

Measures the arc cosine value of a given signal or value.

## Syntax

acos(&lt;signal&gt;|&lt;value&gt;)

## Returns

A signal or scalar value.

## Arguments

```
<signal>|<value>
```

The signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found
- Domain error (&gt;1, &lt;-1)

## Examples

```
acos('0|v(out)') acos(0.6)=927m
```

<!-- image -->

## acosh

## Description

Calculates the hyperbolic arch-cosine of the signal. If the value is out of domain [1, ), a warning message will appear.

## Syntax

acosh(&lt;signal&gt;)

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;

The signal to be measured. The value should be in the range of [1, ).

## asin

Measures the arc sine value of a given signal or value.

## Syntax

asin(&lt;signal&gt;|&lt;value&gt;)

## Returns

A signal or scalar value.

## Arguments

```
<signal>|<value>
```

The signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found
- Domain error (&gt;1, &lt;-1)

## Examples

```
asin('0|v(out)') asin(0.5)=524m
```

<!-- image -->

## asinh

## Description

Calculates the hyperbolic arch-sine of the signal.

## Syntax

asinh(&lt;signal&gt;)

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

```
<signal>
```

The signal to be measured.

## atan

Measures the arc tangent value of a given signal or value.

## Syntax

```
atan(<signal>|<value>)
```

## Returns

A signal or scalar value.

## Arguments

```
<signal>|<value>
```

The signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found

## Examples

```
atan('0|v(out)') atan(10)=1.47
```

<!-- image -->

## atanh

## Description

Calculates the hyperbolic arch- tangent of the signal. If the value is out of domain (-1,1), then a warning will be given.

## Syntax

atanh(&lt;signal&gt;)

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;

The signal to be measured. The value should be in the range of (-1,1).

## complex

Returns a complex scalar or waveform with x as the real part and y as the imaginary part. Both x and y need to be real values or signals.

## Syntax

complex(&lt;real signal&gt;|&lt;value&gt;,&lt;imag signal&gt;|&lt;value&gt;)

## Returns

A signal or scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;real\_signal&gt;|&lt;value&gt;

The real signal or value.

&lt;imag\_signal&gt;|&lt;value&gt;

The imaginary signal or value.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found(Real/Imag)

<!-- image -->

## Examples

```
complex('0|v(out)','0|v(out)') complex(2,3)=0
```

## conjugate

## Description

Returns the conjugate of a complex number. The conjugate of a complex number is a number with opposite sign at the imaginary part.

## Syntax

conjugate(&lt;signal&gt;)

## Returns

A complex signal.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;

The signal to be calculated. Complex signals are supported.

## cos

Measures the cosine value of a given signal or value (in radian units).

## Syntax

cos(&lt;signal&gt;|&lt;value&gt;)

## Returns

A signal or scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;|&lt;value&gt;

The signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found

<!-- image -->

## Examples

```
cos('0|v(out)') cos(60)=-952m
```

## max

Compares at least two (and up to 32) signals or values and calculates the larger of the signals or values.

## Syntax

```
max(<signal1>|<value1>,<signal2>|<value2>,[<signal3>|<value3> ... <signal32>|<value32>])
```

<!-- image -->

## Returns

A signal or scalar value.

## Arguments

```
<signal1>|<value1>
```

The first signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

```
<signal2>|<value2>
```

The second signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

```
<signal3>|<value3> ... <signal32>|<value32>
```

(Optional) The third through thirty-second signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found

## Examples

```
max('0|v(out)','0|v(out)') max(2,3)=3
```

## round

Rounds the given signal or value to an integer value and returns the nearest integer value of the float, double, or long double argument passed to this function. If a decimal value is between .1 and .5 , an integer value less than the argument is returned. If a decimal value is between .6 and .9 , the integer value is greater than the argument.

## Syntax

```
round(<signal>|<value>)
```

## Returns

A signal or scalar value.

## Arguments

```
<signal>|<value>
```

The signal or value to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found

## Examples

```
round('0|v(out)') round(2.6)=3
```

<!-- image -->

## Measurement Functions

This topic contains information on how to use the supported measurement functions.

The following sections summarize the measurement functions available in the Calculator.

| Function   | Description                                                                                                |
|------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| acrmsval   | Returns the accumulated Root Mean Square value for the waveform.                                           |
| avgdev     | Calculates the average deviation of a given signal.                                                        |
| avgfreq    | Calculates the average frequency of a given signal.                                                        |
| bw         | Returns the bandwidth of a given signal when the signal strength drops below a bound dB from its DC value. |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Function    | Description                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| bw3db       | Equivalent to specifying bw(<signal>, 3), where the dB threshold is fixed to 3dB.                                                                     |
| correlation | Calculates the correlation coefficient of the Y values of given signal versus the X values of a given signal.                                         |
| cross       | Calculates the correlation coefficient of the Y values of given signal versus the X values of a given signal.                                         |
| dBCP        | Calculates a 1 dB Compression Point (dBCP).                                                                                                           |
| dBCPh       | Returns the nth order intercept point.                                                                                                                |
| dBCPhVRI    | dB compression point VRI.                                                                                                                             |
| dcgain      | Calculates the X value of a given signal at the min gain.                                                                                             |
| dcgamos     | Calculates the minimum value of a signal equivalent to the min(gain1,gain2) function.                                                                 |
| dcswing     | Calculates the Y value of a given signal at the min gain.                                                                                             |
| delay       | Calculates the time difference between two signals by the edge index and at the specified switching edges.                                            |
| direct_ipn  | Calculates hbac/pac ipn.                                                                                                                              |
| dutycycle   | Calculates the duty cycle of a given period signal at the specified edges of edge indexes.                                                            |
| enb         | Calculates the effective number of bits of a given signal. The FFT is calculated first, then the SNDR.                                                |
| eye_mask    | Adds a mask on to the existing eye object.                                                                                                            |
| falltime    | Calculates the time difference of a given signal between the high y_threshold crossing and the low y_threshold crossing.                              |
| falltrig    | Calculates the X value of the nth falling edge over threshold Y.                                                                                      |
| flatten     | Flattens the given signal with the given parameter as the new x-axis.                                                                                 |
| gain1_f     | Calculates the frequency of a given signal at the signal magnitude, which is 0db(1).                                                                  |
| gain_m      | Calculates the gain margin of a given signal, which is the amount of gain increase or decrease required to make the loop gain unity at the frequency. |

<!-- image -->

| Function                  | Description                                                                                                                                           |
|---------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| gbp                       | Calculates the gain margin of a given signal, which is the amount of gain increase or decrease required to make the loop gain unity at the frequency. |
| get_harmonic_freq         | Calculates the frequency of the nth harmonic.                                                                                                         |
| globalmax                 | Returns the global maximum Y value of all data points for signal.                                                                                     |
| globalmean                | Returns the global discrete mean value of all data points for a signal.                                                                               |
| globalmin                 | Returns the global minimum Y value of all data points for signal.                                                                                     |
| globalstddev              | Returns the global standard deviation value of all data points for signal.                                                                            |
| integ                     | Calculates the integral value of a given signal from x1 to x2.                                                                                        |

| ipnhVRI                   | N dB intercept point VRI.                                                                                                                             |
| mean                      | Calculates the mean value of a given signal or value from x1 to x2.                                                                                   |
| measure_aperture          | Applies the Aperture measurements to the eye object returned from the create_eye function.                                                            |

## acrmsval

Returns the accumulated Root Mean Square value for the waveform. The following

equation is for continuous waveform:

## Syntax

rmsval(&lt;signal&gt;,[&lt;x\_start&gt;],[&lt;x\_stop&gt;])

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;

The signal to be measured.

[&lt;x\_start&gt;]

(Optional) The starting value of X.

[&lt;x\_stop&gt;]

(Optional) The ending value of X.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found
- X value out of range

## avgdev

Calculates the average deviation of a given signal.

## Syntax

avgdev(&lt;signal&gt;)

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;

The signal to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found
- Incorrect signal type

## Examples

```
avgdev('0|v(out)')
```

## avgfreq

Calculates the average frequency of a given signal.

## Syntax

```
avgfreq(<signal>,[<x_start>],[<x_stop>])
```

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

<!-- image -->

## Arguments

```
<signal>
```

The signal to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

```
[<x_start>] (Optional) The starting x value. The default is the signal starting time. [<x_stop>] (Optional) The stopping x value. The default is the signal ending time.
```

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found
- Incorrect signal type
- X value out of range

## Examples

```
avgfreq('0|v(out)') avgfreq('0|v(out)',2n,8n) avgfreq(4)=201M
```

## bw

Returns the bandwidth of a given signal when the signal strength drops below a bound dB from its DC value.

## Syntax

```
bw(<signal>,<db_band>,[<band_type>],[<topline>],[<percent>])
```

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

```
<signal> The signal to be measured. <db_band> The dB threshold.
```

<!-- image -->

```
[<band_type>]
```

(Optional) The type of measurement ( lowpass , highpass , bandpass , or stopband ). The default is lowpass .

```
[<topline>]
```

(Optional) The top line reference ( firstpoint , detect , a dB value, or a percentage value). The default is firstpoint .

```
[<percent>]
```

(Optional) When specified as 1, the &lt;topline&gt; is a percentage value.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found Incorrect signal type
- Db value out of range

## Examples

bw('0|v(out)','lowpass',topline=firstpoint,percent=1)

<!-- image -->

## bw3db

Equivalent to specifying bw(&lt;signal&gt;, 3) , where the dB threshold is fixed to 3dB.

<!-- image -->

## Syntax

bw3db(&lt;signal&gt;,[&lt;band\_type&gt;],[&lt;topline&gt;],[&lt;percent&gt;])

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;

The signal to be measured.

[&lt;band\_type&gt;]

(Optional) The type of measurement ( lowpass , highpass , bandpass , or stopband ). The default is lowpass .

[&lt;topline&gt;]

(Optional) The top line reference ( firstpoint , detect , a dB value, or a percentage value). The default is firstpoint .

[&lt;percent&gt;]

(Optional) When specified as 1, the &lt;topline&gt; is a percentage value.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found.
- Incorrect signal type.
- DB value out of range.

## Examples

bw3db('0|v(out)','lowpass',topline=firstpoint,percent=1)

## cross

Calculate the x-value of a given signal at y value crossing. Supports both positive and negative count indexes. If positive, it will find the cross from the beginning to the end. If negative, it will find the cross from the end to beginning.

## Syntax

```
cross(<signal>,<y_level>,<edge_index>,[<x_start>], [<percent>],[<trigger_type>],[<occurences>], [<output_xAxisType>],[<tolerance>])
```

## Returns

An analog scalar value. The cross( ) function returns the x value of the nth crossing edge over threshold y\_level beginning at x\_start .

## Arguments

```
<signal> The signal to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. <y_level> The threshold of the Y value.
```

<!-- image -->

amplitudes smaller than tolerance.

<!-- image -->

, the

```
<edge_index> An integer value, which can be 0 , 1 , … , n . [<x_start>] (Optional) The starting point of an X value of a signal. [<percent>] (Optional) The percentage value, which can only be 0 or 1 . If specified as 1 y_level is considered a percentage value; if not, Y is not be percentage value. [<trigger_type>] (Optional) The trigger type ( fall , rise , or either ). The fall argument specifies the wave crossing from above the y_level to below the y_threshold. [<occurences>] (Optional) Specifies to retrieve only one occurrence of an overshoot event for the given waveform (single), or all occurrences of overshoot for the given waveform which you can later plot or print (multiple). [<output_xAxisType>] (Optional) Specifies the X axis type of the result waveform. The value can be time or idx. [<tolerance>] (Optional) Determines the threshold crossings and filters crossings with
```

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found. Y value out of range.

## Examples

```
cross('0|v(out)',3,2,2n,1,trig='fall')
```

<!-- image -->

Both positive and negative count indexes are supported. If the count index is positive, the cross is found from the beginning to the end. If the count index is negative, the cross is found from the end to the beginning.

In the following example, the x-value of the second edge from the beginning of the waveform when it crosses the 0.5 level is reported.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

In the following example, the x-value of the second edge from the end of the waveform (or the second-last edge) when it crosses the 0.5 level is reported.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

## dBCP

## Description

Calculates a 1 dB Compression Point (dBCP). When the amplitude of the input signal is small enough, which is almost the same as (linear) AC analysis. When the input signal grows larger, the circuit response is saturated and the output amplitude does not linearly increase.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

You can calculate the 1dB compression point from HB SWEEP results. Sweep the input amplitude and measure the output amplitude. The algorithm includes:

- Calculating the value of gain by using extrapolation point and the waveform y=f(x) .
- Generating a linear function with slope=1: y=x+gain (where gain is known).
- Finding the point on the waveform that satisfies the following parameters: the difference between the Y value of the point (on the waveform) and the Y value of the point (on the linear function) equals N . N is gain decrease (for example, for P1dB , N=1 ; and for P2dB , N=2 .

## Syntax

```
dBCP(<signal>,<gain_decrease>,<extrapolation_point>, [<input|output>])
```

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

```
<signal>
```

The signal to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

```
<gain_decrease>
```

The difference of the Y value between a point on waveform and a point on the y=x+gain linear function.

```
<extrapolation_point>
```

The X value that needs to be input. According to the X value and the y=f(x) input signal, the system gets the Y value and then generates a y=x+gain -&gt; gain=y-x linear function.

```
[<input|output>]
```

(Optional) Option to choose whether the results are input-based or outputbased.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found. Extrapolation point X value out of range.

## Examples

```
dBCP('0|v(out)',2n,4n,'input')
```

<!-- image -->

## dcgain

Calculates the dcgain value of a given signal at the min gain. The min gain is calculated using the d(out)/d(in) equation, where d(out) is the difference in Y value ( y2-y1 ) and d(in) is the difference in X value ( x2-x1) . When this function is executed, a plot of d(out)/d(in) vs d(in) is displayed, which gets the values of d(in) that correspond to each min gain.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Syntax

dcgain(&lt;signal&gt;,&lt;min\_gain&gt;)

## Returns

An analog scalar value.

## Arguments

&lt;signal&gt;

The signal to be calculated. Analog signals are supported. The magnitude is automatically applied for complex signals.

&lt;min\_gain&gt;

The value of d(out)/d(in) .

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found
- DC gain curve does not cross minimum gain level
- Ill-conditioned DC gain curve

## Examples

dcgain('0|v(out)',4n)

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->
