## apgc

## Description

Calculates the available power gain circles (APGC) over S-parameter values and gain values at specified frequency values. The circles are implemented as sweep signals with gain as a parameter if gain sweep is the input, or with frequency as a parameter if multiple frequency values are input.

The result waveform can be one circle if the waveform file is not a sweep waveform file. One gain value is input, and only one frequency value is selected; otherwise, the resulting waveform can be multiple circles.

## Syntax

apgc(&lt;s11&gt;,&lt;s12&gt;,&lt;s21&gt;,&lt;s22&gt;,&lt;gain&gt;,&lt;freq\_list&gt;)

## Returns

A set of circles.

## Arguments

```
<s11> Input S-parameter s11. <s12> Input signal S-parameter s12. <s21> Input signal S-parameter s21. <s22> Input signal S-parameter s22.
```

```
<gain>
```

The gain value in dB units, which can be one single value, two values separated by space in the format of 'step number', which means to sweep gain values from maximum gain value at a loss of 'Step' (Gmax - Step) with 'Number' times, or three values separated by a space in the format of 'start stop step'. The maximum gain value is calculated with associated S-Parameter values at specified frequency values. For example, Gmax=0.6, Step=0.1, Number=2, gain values is {0.5 0.4}.

```
<freq_list>
```

Can be one single value or a list of frequency values separated by a space.

<!-- image -->

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Ga value is greater than Gamax at trace#=' ', freq=' ', Ga=' ', Gamax=' '
- Ga value is greater than Gamax at freq=' ', Ga=' ', Gamax=' '
- Gamax can't be defined, use Gmsg at trace#=' ', freq=' ', K=' ', |delta|=' ''
- Zero again, |S21| is too small at trace#=' ', freq=' ', S21=(' ', ' ')'
- Zero again, |S21| is too small at freq=' ', S21=(' ', ' ')'
- Zero again, |S12| is too small at trace#=' ', freq=' ', S12=(' ', ' ')'
- Zero again, |S12| is too small at freq=' ', S12=(' ', ' ')'
- All frequency values are not in the files
- Signal is not valid or cannot find the loaded signal

## Examples

```
apgc('0|S-Par.S(1,1)','0|S-Par.S(1,2)','0|S-Par.S(2,1)', '0|S-Par.S(2,2)','-30 -20 5','2.3G 4.1G')
```

## harmonic

## Description

Returns the signal value for a specific intermodulation product.

## Syntax

```
harmonic ([signal <string>] [, coeff1 <string>] [, coeff2 <string>] [, coeff3 <string>] [, coeff4 <string>] [, coeff5 <string>]
```

<!-- image -->

```
[, coeff6 <string>] [, coeff7 <string>] [, coeff8 <string>] [, coeff9 <string>] [, coeff10 <string>] [, xUnits <enum>] [, resultType <string> | resultFile <string>] [, resultsDir <string> | testbenchName <string>] [, analysisName <string>] [, params <string>])
```

## Arguments

```
signal
```

(Optional) The signal expression that will be evaluated and reduced to a specific intermodulation product. For exampleFor snac and hbac data, if no coefficients are specified, the entire signal is reformatted such that a plot will display wavelets for each sideband.v(/out) . If a signal expression is not specified, the function returns the intermodulation frequency value.

```
coeff1-coeff10
```

(Optional) The frequency coefficients used to calculate the intermodulation frequency of the target harmonic. The number of coefficients specified must match the number of primary tones in the circuit.

```
xUnits
```

(Optional) Performs conversion of the xAxis units when not a frequency sweep. 'asIs' means no conversion. 'toW' means the xAxis sweep units in the data is in Dbm and will be converted to Watts. 'toDbm' means the xAxis sweep units in the data is in Watts and will be converted to Dbm.

```
Valid values: asIs, isW, isDbm, toW, and toDbm. (Default: asIs) resultType (Optional) The result type. resultsDir (Optional) The directory where the results reside. resultFile (Optional) The result file. testbenchName (Optional) The testbench name. analysisName (Optional) The user-specified name for the analysis.
```

<!-- image -->

params

(Optional) The parameter conditions.

## noisec

## Description

Calculates the noise circle over input Noise Figure values at specified frequency values. The circles are implemented as a sweep signal with noise\_figure as a parameter if multiple noise figures are specified. Frequency is another parameter if multiple frequency values are specified.

Other needed values include NFmin, Rn and Zopt. These values come from signals in the active waveform file (for example, S-Par.NFmin , S-Par.Rn , and S-Par.Zopt . If these signals are not located in a file, the function fails.

The resulting waveform can be one circle if the waveform file is not a sweep waveform file, one noise figure value is input and only one frequency value is input; otherwise, the resulting waveform can be multiple circles.

## Syntax

```
rf('noisec',<noise_figures>,<freq_list>)
```

<!-- image -->

## Returns

A set of circles.

## Arguments

```
<noise_figures>
```

A value in dB scale which can either be a single value or three values separated by space in the format of start stop step .

```
<freq_list>
```

A frequency list which can be one single value or a list of frequency values separated by space.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Signal not found
- Some frequency values are not in the file
- No noise parameter information in the file
- Imaginary radius values at trace#=' ', freq=' ', nf=' ''
- No system impedance Zo in waveform file
- Invalid noise figure inputs

## Examples

rf('noisc','20 50 5','4.1G 5G')

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## opgc

## Description

Calculates the Operating Power Gain Circles over S-parameter values and gain values at specified frequency values. The circles are implemented as sweep signals with gain as a parameter if gain sweep is input or frequency as a parameter if multiple frequency values are input.

The result waveform can be one circle if the waveform file is not a sweep waveform file. One gain value is input if only one frequency value is selected; otherwise, the result waveform can be multiple circles.

## Syntax

opgc(&lt;s11&gt;,&lt;s12&gt;,&lt;s21&gt;,&lt;s22&gt;,&lt;gain&gt;,&lt;freq\_list&gt;)

## Returns

A set of circles.

## Arguments

```
<s11> Input S-parameter s11. <s12> Input signal S-parameter s12. <s21> Input signal S-parameter s21. <s22> Input signal S-parameter s22. <gain>
```

The gain value in dB scale, which can be a single value, two values separated by spaces in the 'step number' format (sweep gain values from maximum gain value at a loss of 'Step' (Gmax - Step) with 'Number' times), or three values separated by a space in the format of 'start stop step'. The maximum gain value is calculated with associated S-Parameter values at specified frequency values. For example, Gmax=0.6 , Step=0.1 , Number=2 , gain values are {0.5 0.4} .

```
<freq_list>
```

Can be one single value or a list of frequency values separated by a space.

## Errors

Possible error messages include:

- Gp value is greater than Gpmax at trace#=' ', freq=' ', Gp=' ', Gpmax=' '
- Gpmax can't be defined, use Gmsg at trace#=' ', freq=' ', K=' ', |delta|=' ''
- S11/S12/S21/S22 is not S-Parameter
- Zero again, |S21| is too small at trace#=' ', freq=' ', S21=(' ', ' ')'
- Zero again, |S21| is too small at freq=' ', S21=(' ', ' ')'
- Zero again, |S12| is too small at trace#=' ', freq=' ', S12=(' ', ' ')'
- Zero again, |S12| is too small at freq=' ', S12=(' ', ' ')'

<!-- image -->

- All frequency values are not in the files
- Signal is not valid or cannot find the loaded signal

## Examples

opgc('0|S-Par.S(1,1)','0|S-Par.S(1,2)','0|S-Par.S(2,1)','0|S-Par.S(2,2)' ,'5 2','2.3G 4.1G')

For a generic multi-port network, the ports are numbered from 1 to N, where N is the total number of ports. For port n, the associated S-parameter definition is in terms of incident and reflected 'power waves', anand bn respectively. The incident power wave for

each port is as follows:

The reflected wave for each port is defined as:

Zpis the diagonal matrix of the complex reference impedance for each port. Zp * is a conjugate of Zp.V and I are the column vectors of the voltage and currents at each port.

An S-parameter matrix can be defined as where S is an NxN matrix containing elements that can be indexed using conventional matrix notation.

## Working With Designs

This chapter details working with designs in the WaveView tool.

## Note:

A WaveView ADV license is required for many of the features accessible from the Design tab.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Importing a Design
- Applying RC Reduction to a Design
- Using DesignView
- Using the Current Debug Tool
- Using SourceView
- Using ConnectionView
- Using SPICE Lint
- Annotating a Netlist
- Cosim

## Importing a Design

## Note:

A WaveView ADV license is required for this feature.

Designs can be imported in the GUI or from the command line.

To import your design from the command line, see Invoking the WaveView Tool With a Design or Netlist.

<!-- image -->

To import your design from the GUI:

1. Choose Import Design from the File or Design tabs.

The Import Design window opens.

<!-- image -->

2. Choose the simulator from which your design originates.

## Note:

While Spectre ® is a supported simulator, it is not displayed in the Simulator menu by default. To add Spectre to the Simulator menu, add the following line to your .cxinit file:

```
cx_simulator_list -add spectre
```

3. Add netlist files.

To add a netlist file, enter the path name of the netlist file in the File text box and click Add , or click Browse to locate one. The file is added to the list of netlist files.

If necessary, you can change the netlist type by clicking in the Type column next to a netlist file name and choosing from the menu of file types that appear.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

4. Add simulator setup files.

To add a simulator setup file, click the Sim. Run Script tab, and either enter the path name of the setup file or browse to its location. Click Import to import the setup file.

5. Add any command-line options in the Command Line Options table.

See Supported Command-Line Options for a list of available command-line options.

6. Use the Design Settings tab to set:
- Power and ground signals
- RC Reduction
- Recognize CMOS gates
- Merge parallel MOS
7. Use the Device Mapping tab to open and save map files or load subciruits from a file.
8. Click OK to import your design.

## Importing Scripts for VCS 3 Step Flow

For VCS 3 step flow, use the Import Design dialog to import both .compile and .elaborate scripts. First, import vcs.compile, then import vcs.elaborate.

<!-- image -->

## Updating a Design

To update a design when imported netlist files are modified outside of the WaveView tool, select the name of a design, and choose Update from the Design tab. The design is recompiled, and any tests are updated.

## Removing a Design

To remove a design, click the design name, and then click Remove on the Design tab.

## Applying RC Reduction to a Design

To apply RC reduction to your design:

1. Click Import Design in the Design section of the Design tab, then select the Design Settings tab.
2. Click the Short Resistor (&lt;) , Open Resistor (&gt;) , or Open Capacitor (&lt;) check boxes to set RC reduction values for those types, then enter the reduction value in the associated text field.
3. Click OK to save your settings.

<!-- image -->

The RC reduction you specify is applied to your design.

## Opening DesignView

To open the DesignView window, click the name of a netlist or design in the Project Hierarchy pane of the Design Import window, and click DesignView from the Design tab. You can also right-click the name of a netlist or design in the Project Hierarchy pane, and choose Open DesignView from the menu that opens.

## Traversing Designs

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Viewing the Design Browser
- Design Display Settings
- Viewing Design Hierarchy
- Viewing Design Cells
- Viewing Design Files
- Filtering Signals, Elements, and Files

## Viewing the Design Browser

When you click on a cell in the Design Browser, which is located in the DesignView window, the following corresponding design elements are displayed:

- Any associated signals, which are listed the bottom half of the Design Browser under the Signal heading
- The associated design netlist with the selected cell portion positioned at the top of the SourceView window
- The subcircuit connections for the selected cell in the ConnectionView pane
- Double-clicking a cell shows the full connection of the cell in the current view (Full Connection mode is activated)

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Design Display Settings

The Browser section of the Design tab selects which parts of your design to display in the File Browser:

- Hierarchy

Displays the full hierarchy of your design.

- Cells

Displays the cells of your design.

- Files

Displays the files associated with your design.

<!-- image -->

## Viewing Design Hierarchy

To view the design hierarchy, click the Hierarchy option on the ribbon. The Design Hierarchy Browser displays the hierarchy tree.

<!-- image -->

## Changing the Design Hierarchy Name Display

To change the design hierarchy name display:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the DesignView category on the left.
3. Choose one of the following display types from the DesignView Hierarchy Name Display section, which controls how instances appear in the Design Hierarchy:
- Instance(Module) Type
- Instance(Module)
- Instance
4. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

## Filtering Design Hierarchy Instances

Before you filter any instances in the Design Hierarchy Browser, consider the following filter rules:

- A new filter always overwrites the previous filter for the same scope.
- Filter strings cannot be used to search within a scope; the text string is treated as a filter string for the currently selected scope.
- Filter strings are not case-sensitive.
- Asterisks (*) and question marks (?) can be used as a wildcard symbol as part of a filter string.

<!-- image -->

To filter instances in the Design Hierarchy Browser:

1. Click a scope level in the hierarchy tree.
2. Type the string you want to filter out in the Filter text box.

<!-- image -->

Other instances are filtered out of the current scope. The filtered name is displayed in brackets, which shows that a particular scope is filtered.

If you do not want to filter instances for a scope with a filtered tag, click that scope in the hierarchy list. The filtered string of the selected scope is displayed and modified or removed.

3. (Optional) Click the down arrow next to the Filter text box to change how the filter works.

<!-- image -->

Clicking the Exclusion check box filters out all instances that contain inputted text instead of displaying them.

Clicking the All Sub-level check box filters all sublevels of a selected node and adds tags for all sublevel instances in the hierarchy tree.

<!-- image -->

## Tracing Through all Hierarchy (in Full Connection Mode)

<!-- image -->

User tracing is allowed in Full Connection mode. Select a signal in the current view and click the Trace Through All Hierarchy button to open a new side-by-side view and trace the selected signal's full hierarchy connection in the new view.

## Viewing Design Cells

To view all the elements for the currently selected cells in a design, click the Cells tab, which is located at the bottom of the Design Browser in the DesignView window.

The Cell List displays all subcircuits and modules in design. Unused cells are listed, but library cells for digital designs are not. The element names and corresponding type are displayed in the Element List.

## Viewing Design Files

To view the files that are associated with your design, click the Files tab, which is located at the far bottom of the Design Browser in the DesignView window. All files are listed in the Design Browser, and all cells in a selected file are listed in the Signal Browser.

The top area of the File Browser displays the imported file structure, and the bottom area displays cells that are defined in the currently selected file.

Signal tracing in the File Browser is limited to the scope of current module.

## Filtering Signals, Elements, and Files

To find a signal, element, or file within the Signal, Element, or File Browser, enter the first few characters of the name in the Filter text box just above the Signal, Element, and File Browser. The full list of signals, elements, or files are filtered, and just those items that match the entered characters are displayed.

## Searching Designs

To search for a signal, instance, cell, or string in the DesignView:

1. Click the binoculars icon in the DesignView toolbar, or click Search on the Design tab.

<!-- image -->

The Find dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Choose the type of item you want to search from the Find menu, and enter a search term in the text box.
3. Choose where you want to search from the In menu.
4. If you choose Cell or String from the Find menu, All Imported Cells or All Imported Files is selected by default in the In menu, respectively. Skip to the next step.

Otherwise, If you choose Signal , Instance , or Instance by Cell , enter the signal or instance you want to find into the text box just to the right of the In menu. toplevel is the default.

Also, if you are searching in the Design Hierarchy , you can click the All sub-level check box to find a match in the current level and all sublevels of the design hierarchy.

5. Click the Find Next button to find the next occurrence of the search term.

The next match to the search term is highlighted in the DesignView and added to the search results.

If you click Find All , all the matched search terms are added to the search results.

<!-- image -->

6. (Optional) Click the Show Results button to display a list of search results.

Each time a search term is matched, its location is added to the list of results. Clicking a search result also highlights the result in the DesignView.

## Generating a Flattened Netlist

To generate a flat netlist from an original netlist:

1. Ensure you have a DesignView open (click DesignView on the Design tab).
2. Hold the Shift key, and drag the selection rectangle over the parts of the design you want to include in the flat netlist.
3. Choose Top-Level Flat Netlist from the menu in the Utilities section of the Design tab.

<!-- image -->

The Flat Netlist dialog box opens.

4. Enter the path to the original netlist in the Save To text box, or browse to its location.
5. (Optional) Unckeck the Output Node mapping information check box if you do not want to include output node mapping information in your flat netlist.

Output node mapping information is included by default.

6. Click Save to flatten the netlist.

## Extracting Measure Statements

To extract .MEASURE statements from a netlist file:

1. Ensure you have a DesignView open (click DesignView on the Design tab).
2. Choose Extract Measure from the menu in the Utilities section of the Design tab.

<!-- image -->

The Extract Measure dialog box opens.

3. Enter the path to where you want to save the extracted .MEASURE statements in the Save To text box, or browse to a location.
4. (Optional) Enter the number of valid digits in the Number of Valid Digits text box. The default is 5.

For example, if the value of parameter A is 3.2 and the number of valid digits is 5 , then parameter A is 3.2000 in the exported file.

5. Click Save to create a W/L report in the selected location.

You can also click Save &amp; Open , which creates the list and opens it in the VI editor.

The extracted .MEASURE statements are exported to a text file, which you can apply to the corresponding simulation files. If the input netlist is a hierarchical netlist with .MEASURE statements embedded inside subcircuits, any parameter or output variable in these .MEASURE statements are resolved before being exported.

The exported netlist file also contains all the necessary .PROBE statements for generating simulation output waveforms. These .PROBE statements are commented out in the extracted file.

For example, when extracting .MEASURE statements from the following netlist:

```
.subckt sub1 1 3 R1 1 2 1K R2 2 3 1K .MEASURE avg_value AVG PAR('V(2)*A') .ends X1 1 0 S1 .param A=3 The result is: .MEASURE X1.avg_value AVG PAR('V(x1.2)*3')
```

```
*.PROBE V(X1.2)
```

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The extracted netlist no longer depends on any parameters since all parameters values are resolved in the exported netlist. If an output variable does not exist in the input netlist, the exported netlist uses its original variable name. For example, when the following netlist is exported:

```
* VDD does not exist in the netlist .MEASURE avg_cur AVG I(VDD) The result is: .MEASURE avg_cur AVG I(VDD)
```

## Extracting PWL Source

To extract and save the PWL source from your design:

1. Ensure you have a DesignView open (click DesignView on the Design tab).
2. Choose Extract PWL Source from the menu in the Utilities section of the Design tab.

<!-- image -->

The Extract PWL Source dialog box opens.

3. Enter the location for the PWL data to be saved, or browse to and select a directory. PWL data is saved in your working directory by default.
4. (Optional) Click the Open PWL Source Waveforms in WaveView check box to also view the PWL source in the WaveView tool.
5. Click Save to save the PWL data, or click Save &amp; Open to both save and view the PWL data.

The PWL data is saved in the specified location, and the data is displayed in the WaveView tool if the Open PWL Source Waveforms in WaveView check box is checked.

## Converting Stimuli

To convert stimuli in a netlist to a special waveform file, which contains waveforms of all of the input voltage or current sources:

1. Ensure you have a DesignView open (click DesignView on the Design tab).
2. Choose Convert Stimuli from the menu in the Utilities section of the Design tab.

<!-- image -->

The Converting Netlist Stimuli dialog box opens.

3. Enter the simulation Time Span value, which specifies the maximum time.
4. Click OK to convert the netlist stimuli.

The output file contains PWL syntax. For example:

```
V1 V PWL DC=NA +0 400m +1n 2.8 +7.5n 2.8 +8.5n 400m +15n 400m R=0 TD=0
```

## Using the Current Debug Tool

For each signal in DesignView, the Current Debug tool can be invoked to display a dialog for the current of all of the signal's connected ports. In this dialog, you can set time or time range, sort, and filter results.

The following sections detail using the Current Debug tool:

- Invoking the Current Debug Tool
- Viewing the Current Debug Dialog Box
- Single Time Point Current vs. Average Current

<!-- image -->

- Setting Time
- Additional Options

## Invoking the Current Debug Tool

From Connection View, right-click on a net or port and select Current Debug on This Signal .

## Viewing the Current Debug Dialog Box

The following figure details the Current Debug dialog box:

<!-- image -->

## Single Time Point Current vs. Average Current

You can choose to show one time point current or time range average current by selecting the corresponding radio box at the top of the dialog window. When choosing Average Current , an additional Time setting line and cursor selection button are shown, as follows:

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Setting Time

You can set time in the dialog window in one of the following ways:

- Input time manually - input the time value in the Time field and press the Enter key to update the results.
- Select time with the cursor in WaveView - click the cursor selection button and in WaveView, either select or create a new cursor to set the time value. The selected cursor is bound to this time setting; if the cursor is moved, the results are updated.

## Additional Options

The following options are also available in the Current Debug dialog window:

- Sort the result table - right-click on a column head in the results table and choose Sort by Ascend or Sort by Descend .
- Filter the result table by current value - right-click on the current value column and select Filter to open a new dialog box where you can input the threshold value. Any current items smaller than this value are removed from the results table.
- Sync highlight port in Connection View - if you select one port in the table, the Connection View will automatically focus to this port and highlight it in the graph. If the port does not exist in the current Connection View, the tool will open a new DesignView to show this port's instance and highlight this port.
- Sync signal from Connection View - when you select another signal or port from the current Connection View, the Current Debug dialog is automatically updated to show new signal's connection result.

Check the SourceView option in the Show section of the Design tab to display the SourceView pane.

## Using Netlists

## Using Bookmarks in your Netlist

You can set bookmarks in your netlist so that you can quickly refer back to specific parts.

This following topics are available in this section:

- Setting Bookmarks
- Traversing Bookmarks
- Removing Bookmarks

## Setting Bookmarks

To set a bookmark, click in the column to the left of the lines in a netlist.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

A red rectangle appears at the beginning of a line that is bookmarked and currently selected. All other lines that contain that a bookmark, but are not currently selected, are marked with a pink rectangle . For example:

## Traversing Bookmarks

<!-- image -->

To move from one set bookmark to the next, click the Previous Bookmark or Next Bookmark buttons, which are located in the SourceView button toolbar.

## Removing Bookmarks

To remove a bookmark, click the red or pink rectangle bookmark symbol next to a bookmarked netlist line.

## Searching Netlists

To search the netlist within the currently selected scope, click the binoculars button in the SourceView button toolbar. Search matches are highlighted in the netlist.

## Hiding Netlist Line Numbers

To hide netlist line numbers in the SourceView:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the SourceView category in the left hand column.
3. Click the Line Number Off check box in the Preference Settings window.
4. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

## Finding Signal Connections

To set a trace, double-click the name of a signal in the netlist.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

A symbol appears at the beginning of a line that contains a currently selected trace signal. All other lines that contain that trace, but are not currently selected, are marked with a symbol.

## Traversing Connections

To traverse through the connection traces you have set in your netlist, click the up or down buttons just above the netlist pane. When a trace is selected in the SourceView, the corresponding connection is highlighted in red in the ConnectionView.

You can also double-click the name of a signal in the SourceView or choose a specific connection trace from the Trace menu located just below the DesignView window menu bar.

<!-- image -->

## Tracing Connections

To display the connections for a trace, right-click a signal, and choose Trace Connectivity from the menu that opens. Blocks that contain the connection are highlighted as turquoise text in the Design Browser.

## Displaying Trace Connections

To display the connections associated with a trace, right-click a signal, and choose Trace Connectivity from the menu that opens. The connections appear in the ConnectionView with the trace node highlighted.

The Trace Connectivity menu options are:

- New View : Always opens a new view to show its connection.
- Append : Adds the signal connection to the current view.
- Replace : Replaces the current view's connection with the signal's connection.

You can also trace multi-net signals by double-clicking a net in the ConnectionView. The connecting net is added to the ConnectionView display.

## Suppressing Out of Scope Warnings

To suppress out of scope warnings:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the DesignView category on the left.
3. Click the Suppress "Out of Scope" Warning for Signal Tracing check box.
4. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

The ConnectionView is the following pane at the bottom of the DesignView window:

## Selecting and Deselecting Items

To select an item, click your mouse button on an item. When you click on another item when one is already selected, any previously selected ones are deselected.

If you want to select more than one item, you can either click an item one at a time while holding the Ctrl key, or you can hold the Ctrl key while drawing a selection rectangle around items you want to select.

To deselect an individual item when multiple items are selected, hold the Ctrl key and click your mouse button on each item you want to deselect. Otherwise, you can deselect multiple items by clicking on one item.

<!-- image -->

## Zooming In and Out

To zoom into the display of your circuit connection, click the Zoom In button in the ConnectionView toolbar, or roll your mouse wheel forward. To zoom into a specific area, hold the Shift key while dragging your mouse pointer to select the section of connections you want to zoom.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

To zoom out, click the Zoom Out button , or roll your mouse wheel backward.

## Viewing Full and Current Hierarchy Connections

The ConnectionView toggles between displaying the full connection hierarchy or the current connection hierarchy.

<!-- image -->

To view the full hierarchy connection when you are viewing the current hierarchy connection, click the button in the upper left corner of the ConnectionView pane.

<!-- image -->

To view the current hierarchy when you are viewing the full hierarchy connection, click the button.

## Viewing the Total Load for Nets

To view the total load for a net, right-click a net in the ConnectionView and choose Signal Loads form the menu that opens. A dialog box opens with the name of the net and total load value displayed.

## Hiding and Showing Instances, Nodes, or Terminals

To hide an instance, node, or terminal, right-click an item in the ConnectionView, and choose Hide Objects from the menu that opens.

To show hidden items, click any open space in the ConnectionView, and choose Show Hidden Objects from the menu that opens.

## Showing Full and All Sub-level Full Connections

To show full connections, select one or more instances, then right-click your mouse and choose Show Full Connections from the menu that opens. The full connections for the selected instances are displayed.

<!-- image -->

To show all sublevel full connections, select one or more instances, then right-click your mouse and choose Show All Sub-level Full Connections from the menu that opens. All instance sublevel connections are displayed.

## Expanding All Sub-Level Instances

To expand all sublevel connections in the selected instance, right-click your mouse and choose Expand All Sub-Level Instances from the menu that opens.

## Showing Single Connections

To show a single connection, right click a connection, and choose Show This Connection Only from the menu that opens.

## Showing Connections Through All Scopes

To show connections through all scopes, choose Show Connection Through All Scopes from the menu that opens.

To trace all ports up to the parent scope in the current view, click the Up arrow after the scope name (or press B ). The connection of the subscope is hidden in the instance box. If there is no port, a warning is displayed.

## Showing Lumped Capacitance

Right-click on a signal and select Show Lumped Capacitance to view the signal's lumped capacitance (the sum of all Cg values connected to this signal).

This is also supported for DSPF. When showing lumped capacitance on the ideal signal (dashed line, in ConnectionView), the tool sums all Cg values inside this ideal signal.

## Working With Hierarchical Labels for Instances or Nodes

You can add hierarchical labels for instances and nodes in the ConnectionView.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Adding Labels
- Moving Labels
- Deleting Labels

## Adding Labels

To add hierarchical labels for instances or nodes, right-click an instance or a node in the ConnectionView, and choose Label Full Hierarchy Name from the menu that opens. A label appears next to the instance or node name with either the full hierarchy or shortened text, which you can set in the preferences.

When you click a label, the instance or node name is also displayed in line editor added in NO.2. If you click a label, both the label and node are highlighted. In the same way, if you click a node, the label is also highlighted.

## Note:

The label display is only for the current schematic sheet. If you change to another sheet, you need to add a new label to the new sheet.

## Moving Labels

To move a label, right-click a label in the ConnectionView, and choose Move from the menu that opens. Move your mouse pointer to the location where you want the label, the click your mouse. The label is moved to the new location.

## Deleting Labels

To delete a label, right-click a label in the ConnectionView, and choose Delete from the menu that opens. The label is removed.

## Calculating Resistance

To calculate resistance and view resistance results in ConnectionView, right-click on a signal or empty space in the ConnectionView window and select Show Point2Point Resistance Value from the context menu.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The Show Point2Point Resistance Value dialog box appears, as follows:

<!-- image -->

In the Show Point2Point Resistance Value dialog box:

1. Use the pick buttons to set Start Point and End Point from a signal or port in ConnectionView. If you used a signal to open the dialog, that signal is automatically populated as the startpoint.
2. Check Color Path and select a color to mark the signal and resistance in ConnectionView after calculating. To remove (or reset) the color, uncheck the Color Path option (to reset the color, uncheck it and check it again).
3. Click Apply .

If the calculation is a success (has a path), all resistance in the path and its resistance value are listed in a table in the bottom of dialog. The resistances are sorted descending as default. Right-click the column header to change sorting method.

## Setting Global VDD and GND Signals

To set global VDD and GND signals in the ConnectionView:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the ConnectionView preference category on the left.

The ConnectionView preferences appear.

3. Enter the types of VDD and GND signals in the VDD Signals and GND Signals text boxes.
4. (Optional) Click the Set Signal Connected with Bulk to VDD or GND check box to set the signals that are connected with bulk to the VDD or GND signals.
5. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

<!-- image -->

## Setting the Maximum Displayed String Length

To set the maximum displayed string length in the ConnectionView:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the ConnectionView preference category on the left.

The ConnectionView preferences appear.

3. Enter the maximum number of characters you want to display for stings in the Max Displayed String Length text box.

A 20 character maximum is specified by default.

4. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

## Setting Parasitic RC Filters

To set a parasitic RC filter in the ConnectionView:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the ConnectionView preference category on the left.

<!-- image -->

The ConnectionView preferences appear.

3. Click the Parasitic RC Filter check box.
4. Enter values for the parasitic resistor and capacitor thresholds in the Parasitic Resistor Threshold and Parasitic Capacitor Threshold text boxes, respectively.
5. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

## Enabling Warnings for Traced VDD or GND Signals

To enable a popup warning for traced VDD or GND signals in the ConnectionView:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the ConnectionView preference category on the left.

The ConnectionView preferences appear.

3. Click the Popup Warning Dialog for Tracing VDD or GND Signals check box.

This preference is enabled by default.

4. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

## Enabling Large Resistors to Be Opened

To enable large resistors (larger than 1e120hm) to be opened in the ConnectionView:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the ConnectionView preference category on the left.

The ConnectionView preferences appear.

3. Click the Open Large Resistors (R &gt; 1e120hm) check box.
4. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Setting Highlighting Style for Selected Instances or Nodes

To set the color and style for instances or nodes you select in the ConnectionView:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the ConnectionView preference category on the left.

The ConnectionView preferences appear.

3. Select a color and line style for instances and nodes in the Highlight Style section at the bottom of the page. The same color is applied while traversing up or down the design hierarchy.

<!-- image -->

The magenta color and solid line is selected by default.

4. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

## Merging Parallel Instances

Enable the preference Merge Parallel MOS to have all instance parameters of the parallel instances merged. The M (multiple) instance parameter is updated with the number of parallel instances.

## Changing ConnectionView Display Settings

You can change how terminals and instances are displayed in the ConnectionView. When you change the display options, all schematic sheets in the ConnectionView are updated.

## Note:

Changes you make to the ConnectionView display are not saved by defaultyou must save your session or design file to save any changes.

## Changing Subcircuit Display

To change how subcircuits are displayed in the ConnectionView:

1. Click in an empty part of the ConnectionView, and choose ConnectionView Display Options from the menu that opens.

The ConnectionView Display Options window opens.

2. Click the plus symbol next to the Show connected terminals only per subcircuit text to display the list of subcircuits in your design.
3. (Optional) To filter specific subcircuits out from the list, enter a filter string, and click Filter .

The asterisk (*) and question mark (?) wildcards are supported.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

4. Click the check box next to a subcircuit name to select a terminals you want to display.

Selected terminals are only displayed when the connection node of a terminal is traced. Other terminals are not displayed in the ConnectionView. Clicking the check box in the heading of the column selects or deselects all subcircuit terminals.

5. Click Apply to apply the display changes to the ConnectionView.

## Changing Instance Visibility Display

To change the visibility of instances in the ConnectionView:

1. Click in an empty part of the ConnectionView, and choose ConnectionView Display Options from the menu that opens.

The ConnectionView Display Options window opens.

2. Click the plus symbol next to the Instance visibility display text to display the list of subcircuits in your design.
3. Click the check box next to an instance name you want to display.
4. Click Apply to apply the display changes to the ConnectionView.

## Displaying Key Bindings

Right-click in ConnectionView and select Show Key Binding Information to display the GUI key bind information.

## Using SPICE Lint

To open the SPICELint window, click SPICELint on the Design tab.

SPICELint screens SPICE netlist files for several problem areas, which can include:

- Syntax errors
- Floating nodes
- Shorted terminals

Netlist properties are also highlighted, which can potentially cause inconsistent simulation behaviors in various simulators.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Selecting Linter Rules and Running the SPICELinter
- Viewing Linter Options

- Viewing Linter Results
- Saving SPICELint Results
- Displaying the LintView on Startup

## Selecting Linter Rules and Running the SPICELinter

To select the rules you want the Linter to use when checking your design and then run the Linter:

1. Click SPICELint on the Design tab.

The Linter window opens.

2. Click the Syntax category in the Lint Options pane.

All Syntax rules are displayed in the Rules table.

3. Select or deselect any rules that you want or do not want to include.
4. Enable or disable any rules for the Connection, ERC Checks, and Parameters rule categories.
5. Click Run to run the Linter.

The Linter closes after the run is complete and the status bar reaches 100%.

Results are displayed in the LintView pane in the DesignView window. See Viewing Linter Results for more information on reading the results.

You can also invoke the Linter from the command line by entering the following line:

```
cx -spicelint <design_netlist_file>
```

## Viewing Linter Options

To view the linter options currently set in the Linter, click SPICELint on the Design tab. The Linter window opens with the options for checking Syntax, Connectivity, ERC Check, or Parameters displayed.

The following SPICELint option categories are available:

- SPICELint Syntax Options
- SPICELint Connectivity Options
- SPICELint ERC Checks Options
- SPICELint Parameter Options

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

See Selecting Linter Rules and Running the SPICELinter for information on how to set the Linter rules.

## SPICELint Syntax Options

You can choose from the following SPICELint Syntax options:

Table 1 Linter Syntax options

| Rule   | Description                            | Type    |
|--------|----------------------------------------|---------|
| SERR   | Syntax error                           | Error   |
| TLE    | Command ignored in title line          | Warning |
| ESM    | .ENDS/.EOS is missing.                 | Warning |
| SOC    | Redundant .ENDS                        | Warning |
| ENE    | Premature .END deck                    | Warning |
| NED    | .END deck is missing                   | Warning |
| LMQ    | Line has missing quote                 | Warning |
| NCR    | Line has no carriage return            | Warning |
| RST    | Redundant slash token                  | Warning |
| FNF    | File not found                         | Warning |
| RLP    | Relative library/included file path    | Warning |
| FRD    | File read denied                       | Error   |
| FRI    | File recursively included              | Error   |
| LEM    | Nested library                         | Warning |
| UEV    | Undefined environment variable in path | Warning |
| SNP    | Subcircuit has no port                 | Warning |
| SPR    | Subcircuit port redefined              | Error   |
| SRD    | Subcircuit is redefined                | Warning |
| UET    | Unknown device type                    | Error   |
| NMD    | Model device name missing              | Error   |
| NMP    | Model name missing                     | Error   |

| Rule   | Description                                     | Type    |
|--------|-------------------------------------------------|---------|
| MRD    | Model redefined                                 | Warning |
| PRD    | Parameter redefined                             | Warning |

## Saving SPICELint Results

When the WaveView tool is launched with the option -dump\_splint with the wv command, results are saved after running SPICELint in the file wv\_splint\_result.txt under the current working directory.

## Displaying the LintView on Startup

To display the LintView pane as part of the DesignView window every time you run WaveView:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

2. Click the DesignView category on the left.
3. Click the Show Lint View on Startup check box.
4. Click Apply to save your settings for just this session, or click Apply-Save to save your preference settings for future sessions.

## Annotating a Netlist

This section contains information on the following items in the Annotation section of the Design tab:

## On/Off

To annotate your netlist with linked waveform data:

1. Click On/Off in the Annotation section of the Design tab.

The green plus sign is displayed in the icon for the On/Off annotation when it not yet on; a red minus sign is displayed when annotation is on.

If you already set up annotations, the annotation values from the linked waveform data appear below each signal in the SourceView. You can skip the remaining steps.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

If you have not set up annotations, click Setup in the Annotation section of the Design tab. The Annotation Setup window opens.

Continue on to the next step.

## 2. Choose what type of time you want to annotate:

- Use Target Signal Change

If the target signal is analog, you can choose Value Change , which jumps to the next or previous time point when the Y-value time point changes (for example, when you click the Previous or Next button when viewing waveform data). Value Change is the default.

If the target signal is digital, you can choose Logic Rise or Logic Fall , which jumps to the next or previous time point depending on the rising or falling edge of the signals (for example, when you click the Previous or Next button when viewing waveform data).

- Use Reference Signal

By default, the referenced signal is the selected signal, but you can also choose another signal as the reference signal.

If the target signal is analog, you can choose Value Change , which jumps to the next or previous time point when the Y-value time point changes (for example, when you click the Previous or Next button when viewing waveform data). Value Change is the default.

If the target signal is digital, you can choose Logic Rise or Logic Fall , which jumps to the next or previous time point depending on the rising or falling edge of the signals (for example, when you click the Previous or Next button when viewing waveform data).

- Use Fixed Time Step

Uses the specified value as a time step instead of the time points in waveform files.

- To Time

Jumps directly to the specified time.

3. (Optional) Click the Use WV Cursor Value check box to change the X-value based on the position of a cursor in the WaveView tool.

<!-- image -->

4. Choose the maximum string width for annotation values, which specifies the number of values that are displayed in the SourceView and ConnectionView:
- User Specified

The default logic value is 8, and the default analog value is 8.

- Same as Signal Name String
5. Enter a value in the Analog Precision Value text box.

The default is 2.

6. Click OK to save the settings.

Annotation values from the linked waveform data appear just below each signal in the SourceView.

## Setup

To change annotations, click Setup in the Annotation section of the Design tab.

For information on an annotation, see Step 2 in On/Off.

<!-- image -->

A checked box means that the waveform file is enabled, and an unchecked box means that the waveform file is not enabled.

This chapter details how to use WaveView editors and tools.

## Using the PWL Editor

To open the PWL Editor, click PWL Editor in the Tools tab.

The PWL Source Editor is used to construct SPICE PWL input stimuli for circuit simulations. The editor supports interactive editing functions via direct point dragging. Multiple sources can be edited or overlapped simultaneously. You can store the edit result in the text PWL storage files (.pwl) or exported to SPICE netlist files.

The buttons are grouped into three groups:

- File Operations
- Source Operations
- Point Operations

## File Operations

Open a prestored PWL editing task with the Open button. Save an editing task with the Save button. The save function automatically appends file extension .pwl to the user- specified file name if the .pwl extension is not used. Click the Check button to check errors in the PWL sources such as overlapping time points.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Click Close to close the PWL editor window. All PWL sources are not removed when the PWL editor window is closed.

## Source Operations

Click the Add New Source button to add a single PWL source or a bus pattern that contains multiple PWL sources. For bus pattern, the usage of high or low levels, cycle time, rise time, and fall time are indicated in the following figure:

<!-- image -->

The source list window keeps a list of all PWL sources. The selected PWL source is the active source highlighted with thick line. Click Modify a Source to modify the name and parameters of the active source. Click Display Source to toggle the active source on and off.

Delete the active source with the Delete a Source button, or clear all sources with the Delete All button.

## Point Operations

A newly added source has five points. Click on a point to select the point as the active point. You can insert a new point after the current active point using the Insert a Point button, or insert a pattern using the Insert Pattern button. A point can also be directly added with the Time and Value text fields and the Add button. The newly added point becomes the active point highlighted with a solid box. With multiple points in a source, click the Next or the Prev button to jump the active point of a source.

<!-- image -->

To shift the entire PWL pattern forward or backward after the active point, click the Shift Pattern button, and drag the active point horizontally to shift the pattern. For example:

<!-- image -->

The Time and Value fields are updated when a new active point is selected. To modify the values of the active point, enter new values and click the Modify button to make the change. You can also change the values of any point by dragging it directly. Dragging a point also selects it as the active point.

Click the Delete a Point button to delete the active point.

To assist point placement, snap functions can be enabled along the horizontal and vertical direction. Enter the preferred snap distance and check the corresponding option button to enable the snap function.

To zoom in an area, click and hold the mouse and move the mouse pointer to select the zoom area. Click the Zoomout button to zoom out or the Full button to reset to full viewing range.

## Using the ADC Toolbox

To open the ADC Toolbox , choose ADC Toolbox from the menu located in the Utilities section of the Waveform tab. Simplified SNR/THD/SNDR/ENOB calculation functions, for sine input signals, are also provided in the FFT dialog box and the equation builder.

The ADC Toolbox is a built-in tool for detailed performance analysis of A-to-D converter designs. Based on simulation output waveform data or measured data, the ADC Toolbox reports the following performance merits:

- DC static characteristics-Histogram, INL/DNL min/max values, and their standard deviations.
- AC dynamic characteristics-Noise parameters SNR, THD, SNDR, SFDR and ENOB and the frequency-domain power spectrum.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Generic Versus Coherent ADC Toolbox
- Overview of the ADC ToolBox
- Input Signal of ADC Toolbox
- DC DNL/INL Analysis
- Sine Input
- Ramp Input
- Number of Sample Points and INL/DNL
- Sampling Frequency and INL/DNL
- AC Analysis: Coherent Sampling Versus Window Sampling
- Coherent Sampling
- Window Sampling
- Exporting the DNL/INL/FFT Results as Waveform Data
- Saving or Loading an Analysis Setup
- Dumping the Contents of the ADC Toolbox
- ADC Toolbox Display Controls
- Sampled Signal Window
- Histogram, DNL, and INL Windows

- DC Static Characteristics

## Generic Versus Coherent ADC Toolbox

Before WaveView version 2004.4, the ADC Toolbox only supports the Coherent sampling method for sine input waveform and the input waveform have their signal amplitude in code values (signal values range from 0 to 2N-1, where N is the number of bits of the design).

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

From release 2004.4, a new generic ADC Toolbox is introduced. The new ADC toolbox accepts input signal in arbitrary amplitude, and a more generic Window sampling method is added to eliminate the need to sample the input sine waveform over integer cycles, which is a requirement of the Coherent sampling method.

To use the original Coherent-only ADC Toolbox, set the SW\_SX\_ORG\_ADC environment variable to 1 in your shell:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

Without setting the SW\_SX\_ORG\_ADC environment variable, the new generic ADC Toolbox is invoked as the default mode.

The new generic ADC Toolbox also allows the AC and the DC analysis to be carried out separately.

## Overview of the ADC ToolBox

The ADC Toolbox window is divided into three tabs: the Input Parameters tab, DC Analysis Result tab, and AC Analysis Result tab.

The Input Parameter tab acquires input parameters from users for an ADC analysis task. The input parameters are divided into four categories: General input signal properties and data sampling parameters, DC analysis parameters, AC analysis parameters, and AC Coherent sampling parameters.

The DC Analysis Result tab displays sampled waveform and DC result including histogram, DNL and INL plots/distribution.

The AC Analysis Result tab displays the FFT spectrum of the sine input waveform and AC figure of merits including SNR/THD/SNDR/SFDR/ENOB.

## Input Signal of ADC Toolbox

The ADC Toolbox accepts the following input signals:

- Sine: Both AC FFT analysis and INL/DNL analysis are available for the sine input type.
- Ramp: Only the INL/DNL analysis is available for the ramp input type.

The input signal of the ADC Toolbox can be an analog signal with arbitrary amplitude ranges, or a digital bus signal representing the digital output code of an ADC design. For digital bus input signal, the bus signal must be displayed in a waveview panel. Drag an analog signal from the Waveform Browser, or a bus signal from a panel to the Signal field in the ADC Toolbox.

The input signal is sampled based on one group of the following three sampling parameters: Start Time, Stop Time, and number of points, or Start Time, Sampling Frequency (Fs), and number of points. When the stop time is used (in the first group), the last sample point is at:

<!-- image -->

```
stop_time - (stop_time - start_time)/number_of_points
```

For sine input type, the input frequency (Fin) also needs to be specified.

You can input analog bus signals directly by entering bus named delimied by semicolons (;). For example:

```
ADCOUT_3;ADCOUT_2;ADCOUT_1;ADCOUT_0
```

When you enter analog bus signals directly, the following requirements must be satisfied:

- Signals must be analog.
- The number of signals must be the same as the number of bits.
- The order bus signals must be MSB ; .... ; LSB.
- All signals in the bus must come from the same file.
- No more than 32 signals can be entered at a time.

Once the input signals are accepted, the median signal value among all signals is used as the A2D conversion threshold. For example:

```
0.5 * (ymax_of_all_bit + ymin_of_all_bits)
```

The analog bus signals are then converted to a logic bus whose code values are then used as the input to the ADC Toolbox. Analog bus signals are also supported during .INI file save/load operations.

For measured data that was sampled at known Fs, the data (x,y) value pair can use integer index as the x values. If this is the case, select the Measured data option and the ADC Toolbox processes the input as if the data is sampled at Fs. When the Measured Data option is selected, the Start T/P value is the starting index (0-based) of the measured data.

If you have a measurement data with only single column, (that is, the data is measured at fixed known sampling rate so the data file does not contain x-axis sample time information), edit the file header to add the following lines:

```
#format table data_only name_of_data measure data 1 measure data 2 …..
```

<!-- image -->

With the keywords in the header line, the WaveView tool can load such a text data file as a regular waveform file and automatically assign integer index to the x-axis. You can then apply the Measured Data option and use the measurement data in the ADC Toolbox.

## DC DNL/INL Analysis

To calculate DNL/INL, an analog input signal is first scaled into full code range based on the Code Range parameters in the DC Input Parameters section. If the Number of Bits value is used, the ADC Toolbox assumes that the input signal covers full code range from 0 to 2N-1. If the User-defined Code Range option is selected, the ADC Toolbox assumes that the input signal swings from the Min code value to the Max code value. Digital input bus signal is not subject to this amplitude scaling, instead the bus direct code values are used.

If the analog input signal value is already converted to the A/D converter output bus values, select the Signal Value=Output Code option.

Because the ADC Toolbox always automatically scales the analog input signal, PWL sampling is always used in sampling analog input signal.

After entering the necessary DC analysis parameters, click Evaluate DC to carry out a DC analysis.

## Sine Input

For sine input signal, based on the sampled data and the Fin parameters, the ADC Toolbox needs to find the ideal sine wave to calculate INL and DNL. The ADC Toolbox uses two methods to calculate the ideal sine waveform:

- FFT fitting: If the input sine waveform data is not clipped. The amplitude and phase of the strongest FFT spectrum component of the input sine signal is used as the ideal sine waveform.
- LMS (least-mean-square) fitting: If the input sine waveform data is clipped. This is often seen with measure data. The ADC Toolbox uses the sample data within the ClipMin and Clip-Max code values, and LMS fitting method to find the original ideal sine waveform. The offset and the amplitude of the fitted ideal sine waveform is displayed in the Sampled Data plot.

With the LMS fitting, since the clipped sampled data might be heavily distorted, FFT AC analysis is disabled.

## Ramp Input

For the ramp input type, ADC Toolbox always assumes that the ideal ramp signal evenly covers the full code range. Based on this assumption, multiple complete cycles of ramp (up or/and down) are accepted.

## Number of Sample Points and INL/DNL

In order to produce meaningful INL/DNL result, the number of sample points must be large enough so that there is at least one sample point in each code value. For example, for a 10-bit design, ramp input, at least 1024 points (210) sample points are needed. Sine input type needs even more points because the sample points do not distribute evenly over different code values.

Since the ADC Toolbox scales the original analog input signal and uses PWL method to sample the scaled input signal, it is the user's responsibility to make sure that the measurement/simulation generates enough true data points at each code value.

## Sampling Frequency and INL/DNL

For sine input type, if multiple periods of the input sine waveform are sampled, the sampling frequency Fs and input frequency Fin must be carefully selected to avoid sampling the same code values in each period. For example, if a 5 MHz input sine waveform (6-bit) is sampled at 40 MHz over 128 cycles, the 8 sampled code values from each cycle are always the same. As a result, only 8 out of the 64 code values are available in the sampled data. If Fin is at 4.99 MHz, with the sampling frequency, the sampled data has different code values from cycle-to-cycle, and the INL/DNL result would be more meaningful.

## AC Analysis: Coherent Sampling Versus Window Sampling

With the sine input type, the ADC Toolbox supports FFT AC analysis using two different types of sampling method:

- Coherent Sampling
- Window Sampling

## Coherent Sampling

With coherent sampling, exact integer multiple cycles (FinNUM) of the input sine wave are sampled. The sampled data is then sorted into a single cycle of sine wave before performing the dynamic performance analysis using FFT.

<!-- image -->

Advantages of the coherent sampling method include:

- It allows an input signal at higher frequency to be sampled using a lower sampling rate. In the real world, physical measurement equipment might sometimes have limited sampling performance to meet the Nyquist criterion required by the bandwidth of the input signal.
- Harmonics and noise are readily separated in the power spectrum using coherent sampling.
- FFT windowing functions are not required because integer cycles of the input signal are sampled.

Figure 4 Coherent sine wave sampling

<!-- image -->

However, coherent sampling method does require the exact frequency (Fin) of the input sine wave to be known prior to running an ADC simulation. To use the coherent sampling method in the ADC Toolbox, you need to enter the preferred Precision, the estimated Fin and Fclk, and Sample Pts. Then, click Evaluate AC to find out the exact values for Fin.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Figure 4 is a coherent sampling example with FinNUM = 3, N=32. Coherent sampling requires that N x Fclk = FinNUM x Fin. In order to sort sampled points of multiple cycles into a single sine wave cycle, N and FinNUM cannot have any common factor. Since N is always power of 2, an odd number for FinNUM is always a valid choice. In the ADC Toolbox, the FinNUM value can be automatically determined based on user-defined Fin and Fclk values.

As depicted in the above graph, the power spectrum of the sorted sine wave is also a sorted version of the original multi-cycle sine waveform's power spectrum.

The sorted single-cycle sine wave is sometime also referred to as the unfolded sine wave.

Refer to Using the Coherent Sample Only (CSO) ADC Toolbox for details about entering parameters for Coherent Sample.

## Window Sampling

The window sampling method does not require integer number of cycles of the input sine signal to be sampled. However, to overcome the spectral leakage problem from not sampling over an integer cycles of the input waveform, a FFT windowing function is required. Figure 5 shows the FFT spectrum of a 4.99 MHz sine signal sampled over 127.75 cycles at 40 MHz.

Figure 5 FFT Spectrum With Window Functions

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

As depicted in the above spectrum, the power at the fundamental frequency (4.99 MHz) gets spread into neighboring spectral components due to spectral leakage. For this reason, a binsize parameter is required to include all neighboring components within +/binsize spectral range as part of the original fundamental (or harmonic) components. The default of BinSize is 10.

After entering the necessary AC analysis parameters, click Evaluate AC to start an AC analysis.

## Exporting the DNL/INL/FFT Results as Waveform Data

The ADC Toolbox result, including the sampled waveform data, histogram, INL/DNL and the FFT power spectrum, can be exported to a waveview window for further viewing purpose. Click Waveform next to the plot window to display the data into a new waveview window.

## Saving or Loading an Analysis Setup

The ADC Toolbox setup, including the input parameters, sampled data, and the analysis result can be saved into data files. To restore a previously saved setup, load from the .INI (Input parameter) file.

## Dumping the Contents of the ADC Toolbox

To output the contents of the ADC Toolbox to a graphic file (PNG, JPG, or BMP), click the Dump button on the ADC Toolbox window.

## ADC Toolbox Display Controls

The following window displays are included in the ADC toolbox:

## Sampled Signal Window

The Sampled Signal window displays the sampled data waveform based on the input parameters. The y-axis is in code value, with min-code value at the bottom and max-code value at the top.

## Ideal/Acquired/Error/All switch:

- Ideal: Displays the ideal signal used for INL/DNL calculation.
- Acquired: Displays the sampled waveform data.

- Error: Displays the error between ideal signal and the sampled data.
- All: Displays all of the above.

## Sin/Cos/Original (sine input only):

- Sin: Adjusts the phase of the displayed waveform into Sin phase (starts from zero).
- Cos: Adjusts the phase of the displayed waveform into Cos phase (starts from the maximum value).
- Original: No phase adjust for sampled waveform display.

## Exp/Integer:

- Exp: Displays the y-axis value ranges using the engineering format.
- Integer: Displays the y-axis value ranges using the integer code values.

## Histogram, DNL, and INL Windows

These windows display the histogram, DNLb, and INL plots of the sampled signal. Aligned with the y-axis of the Sampled signal plot, the y-axes of all three plots correspond to the code value. The x-axis is the histogram / DNL / INL value in LSB.

## Power Spectrum (Sine Input Only)

The power spectrum window displays the noise spectrum of the sampled signal.

## Line/Bar/Both

- Line: Plots the power spectrum using line chart.
- Bar: Plots the power spectrum using bar chart.
- Both: Plots the power spectrum using both line and bar chart.

## Index/Frequency

- Index: Displays the spectrum x-axis value range using harmonic index.
- Frequency: Displays the spectrum x-axis value range using frequency.

<!-- image -->

## AC Dynamic Characteristics

The AC Characteristics window displays the spectrum harmonic strength and the following values:

- SNR: The signal-to-noise ratio.
- THD: The total harmonic distortion.
- ENOB: The effective number of bits.
- SNDR: The signal-to-noise and distortion ratio.
- SFDR: The spurious free dynamic range. The harmonic index of the second strongest harmonic component is also displayed together with the SFDR value (for example, SFDR index\_after\_sorting (index\_before\_sorting)).

The strength of the power spectrum is in db relative to the strongest harmonic component (0 db for the strongest harmonic component). The AC characteristic window lists the value of each of the harmonic component. Use the up and down buttons to scroll up/down to view the spectrum values at different harmonic range.

Select the toggle check box next to a harmonic component to either exclude the harmonic for the THD calculation or include the harmonic for the SNR calculation.

Click Evaluate AC to update the AC noise analysis result (SNR/THD/ENOB/SNDR/SFDR) based on the new harmonic selection.

## DC Static Characteristics

The DC Characteristics window displays the min/max values and the standard deviation of the INL/DNL distribution. The unit is 1 LSB.

## Running Batch-mode ADC Analyses

ADC Toolbox analysis can be run in batch mode with the -adcin, -adcout,

-adcwdf, and -adccsv command line option. The usage is:

```
wv -adcin adc.INI -adcout out_sw -adcwdf wdf_sw
```

The adc.INI is a previously saved .INI file, out\_sw is the \_ (underscore) delimited type switch that controls the output text files; wdf\_sw is the \_ (underscore) delimited type switch that controls the output WDF waveform files. The -adccsv option sets the output text file in the CSV (comma separated values) format.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

One of the -adcout and -adcwdf options must be specified or the batch mode operation is terminated. Supported type strings are INL, DNL, FFT, TLA, HIS, IND, ALL, and DAT (-adcout only). FFT and TLA have no effect on ramp input signals. For example:

wv -adcin adc.INI -adcout INL\_DNL -adcwdf TLA\_FFT -adccsv
