## Input Signal Requirements

The input waveform for the CSO ADC Toolbox must have its signal strength in integer code values (for example, 0 to 63 for a 6-bit ADC). Run a simulation on an ADC design first and then convert the ADC output codes into an acceptable waveform.

## Preparing the Input Waveform

As depicted in the flowchart below, the following steps demonstrate how to use the WaveView tool to convert the simulated ADC output code (in analog waveforms) to an acceptable input signal for the CSO ADC Toolbox.

Figure 6 Preparing an input signal for the ADC toolbox

<!-- image -->

To convert the simulated ADC output code to an acceptable input signal for the CSO ADC Toolbox:

1. Identify the analog output waveforms that represent the ADC output code, for example, "ad0" to "ad5" for a 6-bit design.
2. Display these signals in a waveview window and then highlight them by highlighting the panels these signals reside in.
3. Use the A/D converter tool in the WaveView single-bit mode to convert each of the highlighted analog waveforms to a digital waveform. Name the converted digital waveforms "AD0" - "AD5", and ensure proper threshold value is used for this A to D conversion step.
4. Group the converted logic signal "AD0" - "AD5" into a digital bus signal. Make sure that the signals are ordered (sorted) correctly so "AD5" is the MSB and "AD0" is the LSB.
5. Rename the grouped bus signal to "AD". You can use this logic bus signal directly as the input to the ADC Toolbox, or you can continue to Step 6.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

To use the logic bus signal as the input, the bus signal must be displayed in a waveview window, and you must drag and drop the logic bus signal from the display panel.

6. Use the D/A convertor tool in the WaveView tool to convert the grouped converted digital bus "AD", in multi-bit mode, into an analog waveform.
7. Ensure that the Use logic bus value option is selected so that the converted waveform has strength in code value.
8. Rename the final analog waveform "ad".

The analog waveform "ad" is now ready for use with the ADC Toolbox. Skip Step 1 to Step 3 if your simulator generates logic output waveforms directly. If your simulator directly generates a logic bus waveform, skip Step 1 to Step 5.

To specify the input signal, drag and drop the converted analog signal from the Waveform Browser to the Signal field in the ADC Toolbox.

## Sampling the Input Waveform

The CSO ADC Toolbox samples the input signal waveform based on the following equation:

## where:

- N is the number of sampling points (power of 2)
- Fin is the input frequency
- FinNUM is the total number of cycles of a sine signal input used for coherent sampling.
- Fclk is the sampling frequency

## Note:

N and FinNUM must not have any common factors.

For sine wave input, the number of sample points N must to be power of 2 because FFT is used internally to calculate the ADC dynamic performance. It is important to choose a value for N, which is large enough to produce at least one sample point for each output code value. In the ADC Toolbox, PWC sampling is always used to sample the input signal waveform.

## Preparing Test Benches for the CSO ADC Toolbox

To maximize the effectiveness of the CSO ADC Toolbox, the following guidelines can be used to prepare the input test tone for simulating an ADC design.

## Input Signal Strength

For both ramp and sine input type, the ideal input signal strength drives the ADC output over a full swing output code from 0 to 2^BIT-1, where BIT is the number of bits. On the other hand, the input signal cannot be too strong, because it can overdrive the ADC outside its operating range. Proper input signal strength results in more accurate INL/DNL analysis results.

## Input Sine Wave Frequency

In general, depending on the speed performance of the ADC design, the input test tone frequency might be low enough so that the digital output does not skip codes. (All output codes can be exercised by the input test tone.) For coherent sine wave sampling, the exact input test tone frequency Fin must be determined before running the ADC simulation.

## CSO ADC Toolbox User Interface

The CSO ADC Toolbox accepts user input parameters and generates graphic and textual analysis report.

After completing an analysis based on user input parameters, the CSO ADC Toolbox allows you to perform the following actions:

- Display analysis results in regular waveview windows
- Export analysis result to text files
- Save/load the analysis parameters setup

## Input Parameters

The following table summarizes the input parameters required by the CSO ADC Toolbox.

| Input Signal Type   | Sine      | Ramp         |
|---------------------|-----------|--------------|
| Start Time          | mandatory | mandatory    |
| Precision           | mandatory | not required |

<!-- image -->

| Input Signal Type   | Sine      | Ramp         |
|---------------------|-----------|--------------|
| Decimation          | mandatory | not required |
| Sample Points       | mandatory | mandatory    |
| Fclk User           | mandatory | mandatory    |
| Fin User            | mandatory | not required |
| Fin #               | optional  | not required |
| Fclk                | optional  | not required |
| Fin                 | optional  | not required |
| Bits                | mandatory | mandatory    |
| THD                 | mandatory | not required |
| SNR                 | mandatory | not required |

- Start Time: The time at which the ADC Toolbox starts sampling the input signal.
- Precision: Number of digits after the decimal point for the internal Fclk, Fin and Fin# calculation. For the sine wave coherent sampling method, small error in Fclk and Fin can result in inaccurate analysis result. If the Use user Fclk/Fin option is not selected, the ADC Toolbox recalculates the precise values internally for Fclk, Fin, and Fin#.
- Decimation: Integer decimation-in-time. Default is 1. The decimation is used to mimic the sampling speed limitation of real measurement equipment by slowing down the sampling clock by the integer decimation factor. The actual sampling clock frequency is Fclk/decimation. When the ADC Toolbox is used on simulation data, set the value to 1.
- Sample Points: Number of sample points. Since the ADC Toolbox uses FFT for noise analysis, the number of sample points must be power of 2.
- Fclk user: The frequency of the sampling clock.
- Fin user: The frequency of the input sine wave. Ignored for ramp input.
- FinNUM: The total integer number of cycles of input sine signal for coherent sampling. Required only when the Use user Fclk/Fin option is selected. It is otherwise calculated internally based on other input parameters. Ignored for ramp input.

## Note:

If the Use user Fclk/Fin option is selected, the Fclk-user value is used directly as the sampling frequency for acquiring data from the input signal. The input data is sampled for a total span of Sample-points / Fclk-user.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

If the Use user Fclk/Fin option is not selected, the ADC Toolbox uses Precision, Fin-User, Fclk-User, Sample Points, and Decimation to calculate the precise internal Fclk, Fin, and FinNUM. In this case, you only need to provide approximate Fclk and Fin values. The final internally calculated Fclk, Fin, and FinNUM values are displayed in corresponding fields.

- Bits/Min/Max: Number of bits of the AD converter design, and the minimal and maximal code value (MIN/MAX). The MIN/MAX values, instead of the Bits value, are used if the Use Code Value Range option is selected. If the Use Code Value Range option is not selected, the Bits value is used and the code value is assumed to range from 0 to 2^Bits - 1. Any sampled code values that are outside this range are clipped at the MIN/ MAX values.
- THD: The highest harmonic order that is included as harmonic for the total harmonic distortion calculation.
- SNR: The highest harmonic order that is excluded from noise for the signal -to-noise ratio calculation.
- Indexed Data: If the input data has been sampled at a fixed rate without the x-axis time information for each of the data points (for example, measurement data), select this option and the ADC Toolbox assumes that the data is sampled at Fclk.

After entering all the required input parameters and the options, click Evaluate to complete the analysis.

## Selecting Sampling Parameters

The following sampling parameters are available:

- Sine Input
- Ramp Input

## Sine Input

To select a sine input sampling parameter:

1. Select the Sine option.
2. Enter a Sample Pts value.
3. If the Use user Fclk/Fin option is selected, enter proper Fclk, Fin, and FinNUM values. These values are used directly by the waveform sampling process.
4. If the Use user Fclk/Fin option is selected, enter proper Fclk, Fin, and FinNUM values. These values are used directly by the waveform sampling process.

<!-- image -->

5. If the Use user Fclk/Fin option is not selected, enter the preferred Precision value and estimated Fclk and Fin values. The FinNUM value and the exact Fclk and Fin values are calculated automatically.
6. Select the Sort Sampled Points option to view the unfolded power spectrum of the sorted sampled waveform, or de-select the Sort Sampled Points option to view the folded power spectrum of the unsorted sampled waveform. You need to click Evaluate every time the Sort Sampled Points option is changed.

## Ramp Input

Select the Ramp option and enter the Start, Sample-Pts, and Fclk values.

## Exporting DNL/INL/FFT Results as Waveform Data

The ADC Toolbox result, including the sampled waveform data, histogram, INL/DNL and the FFT power spectrum, can be exported to a waveview window for further viewing purpose. Select the preferred data type switches in the ADC Toolbox and click Waveform to display the data into a new waveview window.

## Saving or Loading an Analysis Setup

The ADC Toolbox setup, including the input parameters, sampled data and the analysis result can be saved into data files. To restore a previously saved setup, load from the .INI (Input parameter) file.

## ADC Toolbox Display Controls

The following ADC toolbox display controls are available:

- Sampled Signal Window
- Histogram, DNL, and INL Windows
- Power Spectrum (Sine Input Only)

## Sampled Signal Window

The Sampled Signal window displays the sampled data waveform based on the input parameters. The y-axis is in code value, with min-code value at the bottom and max-code value at the top.

## Ideal/Acquired/Error/All switch:

- Ideal: Display the ideal signal used for INL/DNL calculation.
- Acquired: Display the sampled waveform data.
- Error: Display the error between ideal signal and the sampled data.
- All: Display all of the above.

## Sin/Cos/Original (sine input only)

- Sin: Adjust the phase of the displayed waveform into Sin phase (starts from zero).
- Cos: Adjust the phase of the displayed waveform into Cos phase (starts from the maximum value).
- Original: No phase adjust for sampled waveform display.

## Exp/Integer

- Exp: Display the y-axis value ranges using the engineering format
- Integer: Display the y-axis value ranges using the integer code values

## Histogram, DNL, and INL Windows

Theses windows display the histogram, DNL, and INL plots of the sampled signal. Aligned with the y-axis of the Sampled Signal plot, the y-axes of all three plots correspond to the code value. The x-axis is the histogram / DNL / INL value in LSB.

## Power Spectrum (Sine Input Only)

The power spectrum window displays the noise spectrum of the sampled signal.

## Line/Bar/Both

- Line: Plot the power spectrum using line chart.
- Bar: Plot the power spectrum using bar chart.
- Both: Plot the power spectrum using both line and bar chart.

## Index/Frequency

- Index: Display the spectrum x-axis value range using harmonic index.
- Frequency: Display the spectrum x-axis value range using frequency.

<!-- image -->

## AC Dynamic Characteristics

The AC Characteristics window displays the spectrum harmonic strength and the following values:

- SNR: The signal-to-noise ratio
- THD: The total harmonic distortion
- ENOB: The effective number of bits
- SNDR: The signal to noise and distortion ratio
- SFDR: The spurious free dynamic range. The harmonic index of the second strongest harmonic component is also displayed together with the SFDR value (for example, SFDR index\_after\_sorting (index\_before\_sorting)).

The strength of the power spectrum is in db relative to the strongest harmonic component (for example, 0 db for the strongest harmonic component). The AC characteristic window lists the value of each of the harmonic component. Use the up or down buttons to scroll up/down to view the spectrum values at different harmonic range. Select the toggle check box next to a harmonic component to exclude the harmonic for the THD calculation or include the harmonic for the SNR calculation.

Click Evaluate to update the AC noise analysis result (SNR/THD/ENOB/SNDR/SFDR) based on the new harmonic selection.

## DC Static Characteristics

The DC Characteristics window displays the min/max values and the standard deviation of the INL/DNL distribution. The value is in LSB units.

## Loading CircuitCheck Error Reports

## Exporting CircuitCheck Error Reports

1. In the CCK Result Viewer window, choose File &gt; Export CCK Result File .

3. Choose a name for the exported report, and click OK .

The error report is exported and saved to the location you selected.

## Setting the Initial Design Bit Rate

To set the initial design bit rate:

## Setting the Initial Resistance for Terminating Pins

To set the initial resistance for terminating pins:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.
2. The Preference Settings window opens.
2. Click the Channel Sim. &amp; Analysis preference category in the Preferences navigation pane.

The Channel Simulation and Analysis preferences are displayed.

3. Enter an initial resistance value for terminating pins in the Initial Appropriate Resistance for Terminating Pins (ohms) text box.
2. 50 is the default initial resistance value.

## Saving Testbench Stages When Exiting CSA

To save the current testbench stages to an initial file when you exit CSA:

1. Click Settings on the Configuration tab.

The Preference Settings window opens.

<!-- image -->

2. Click the Channel Sim. &amp; Analysis preference category in the Preferences navigation pane.

The Channel Simulation and Analysis preferences are displayed.

3. Click the Save Current Series of Testbench Stages to Initial File When Exiting CSA check box to enable the option.

This option is disabled by default.

4. Click the Apply button to save your changes.

The current series of testbench stages are now saved to your .cxinit file when CSA is closed using the following format:

```
cx_init_stages stage1 stage2 … stageN For example: cx_init_stages Input TxPkg PCB RxPkg Output
```

## Working With Testbench Stages

When you set up testbench stages, you can also configure the order in which they are simulated.

<!-- image -->

You must adhere to the following rules when setting up testbench stages:

- The Input stage is always the first stage, and you cannot delete or move the Input stage.
- The Output stage is always the last stage, and you cannot delete or move the Output stage.
- No more than one Input stage and one Input can exist in one testbench setup.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Adding and Deleting Stages
- Changing Stage Order
- Renaming Stages

## Adding and Deleting Stages

To add a testbench stage:

1. Click Testbench in the navigation pane.

The Setup tab is displayed with all the currently enabled stages in the order of simulation.

<!-- image -->

2. Click the Add button in the upper-left corner of a stage section, and choose a stage type from the menu that appears.

A stage is added just before the Add button you use, and the stage name is also added to the list of stages in the Navigation pane. A block diagram of the new channel connection is also displayed.

## Note:

The Output stage is not available if you already have an Output stage included in your testbench.

<!-- image -->

To delete a stage, click the button at the right-hand side of a stage section. The stage is removed from the Navigation pane, and the block diagram is updated.

## Changing Stage Order

To change the order of stages, right-click a stage name in the Navigation pane, and choose Move Up or Move Down from the menu that opens. The stage moves one position up or down, respectively.

## Note:

The stage just after the Input stage cannot be moved up, and the stage just before the Output stage cannot be moved down.

## Renaming Stages

To rename a stage:

1. Click Testbench in the navigation pane.

The Setup tab is displayed with all the currently enabled stages in the order of simulation.

2. Double-click a stage name in the block diagram.

<!-- image -->

The stage name is highlighted, and a text box opens around the stage name.

## Note:

If you choose a stage name that is too long to display in the ConnectionView, only the beginning and ending characters of the stage name are displayed with an ellipsis in the middle. Hover your mouse pointer over the shortened stage name to view the full stage name.

3. Enter a new name, and press the Return key.

The new stage name is saved.

If you choose Subckt , skip to Step 7.

If you choose Through , skip to Step 8.

3. Choose a buffer from the Buffer menu.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

4. Choose a model from the Model menu, or click the icon to browse to and load a model file.
5. Enter any additional options under any of the sub categories under the Additional Options section.

See the HSPICE® User Guide: Signal Integrity Modeling and Analysis for more information on these additional options.

Skip to Step 8.

6. Enter an element prefix in the Element Prefix text field.

The b\_input text is the Element Prefix by default.

7. Choose a subcircuit from the Subckt menu, or click the icon to browse to and load a subcircuit file.
8. The setup for the Buffer Options is complete.

<!-- image -->

If you choose P Element , continue to the next step.

If you choose Subckt , skip to Step 6.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Skip to Step 7.

## Working With the CS Connection View

The CS Connection View displays the current connections for which you are setting up an CS testbench. You can access the CS Connection View via the Connection tab from the Setup panel for any testbench setup option in the Navigation panel.

<!-- image -->

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Changing Pin Direction
- Adding Connections
- Inserting Devices
- Connecting a Device to Ground
- Inserting Dummy Ports
- Terminating Pins
- Deleting Devices or Pins
- Viewing the Device Setup
- Zooming In and Out
- Zooming to Fit
- Resetting the CS Connection View Display

## Changing Pin Direction

To change the direction of a pin in the CS Connection View, right-click a pin, and choose Change Pin Direction from the menu that opens.

## Adding Connections

To add a connection in the CS Connection View, right-click a pin, and choose Add Connection from the menu that opens. Left-click another pin to complete the connection.

<!-- image -->

## Inserting Devices

To insert a device in the CS Connection View:

1. Right-click anywhere in the Connection View pane, and choose Insert Device from the menu that opens.

The Insert Device dialog box opens.

2. Choose an element from the Element menu.
3. Enter a name for the device in the Name text field.
4. Choose a device category from the Category menu.

The category varies depending on what kind of element you choose.

For information on the elements or categories, see the HSPICE® User Guide: Signal Integrity Modeling and Analysis .

5. Click OK to save your settings.

The device is added to the CS Connection View.

## Connecting a Device to Ground

To connect a device to ground in the CS Connection View, right-click a device, and choose Connect to GND from the menu that opens.

## Inserting Dummy Ports

To insert a dummy Port in the CS Connection View, right-click a connection, and choose Insert Dummy Port from the menu that opens. A dummy port is added to the Connection View.

You can also add dummy ports via stateye analysis setup.

## Terminating Pins

To terminate a pin, right-click a pin, and either choose Terminate Pin from the menu that opens or click the Terminate Pin button in the button toolbar.

## Deleting Devices or Pins

To delete a pin or device in the CS Connection View, right-click a pin or device, and choose Delete from the menu that opens.

## Viewing the Device Setup

To view the settings for a device in the CS Connection View, right-click a device, and choose Device Setup from the menu that opens. The Setup panel opens with the device settings for the selected device.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Zooming In and Out

To zoom into a connection in the CS Connection View, click the button in the button

toolbar.

<!-- image -->

To zoom out, click the button.

## Zooming to Fit

<!-- image -->

To zoom the display to fit the size of your connections in the CS Connection View, click the button in the button toolbar.

## Resetting the CS Connection View Display

To reset the CS Connection View display, click the button in the button toolbar. All devices and connections revert back to their original state.

## Specifying General CS Simulation Settings

To start setting up your CS simulation:

1. Click the Simulation Setup category in the Navigation panel.

The Setup panel displays the general simulation settings.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Enter the path to a simulator executable file in the Executable text box if different configuration settings exist for the simulator, or click the button to browse to and select one.
3. Enter any extra command arguments for running a simulation in the Options text box.
4. Enter any comments you want to include in the netlist in the Comments text box.

## Adding CS Model Files

To add CS model files:

1. Click Model and Include Files in the Navigation panel.

The Model and Include files tab page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

2. Click the Model Files tab.

The Model Files tab page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

3. Double-click the "Click to add" text, and either enter the path to a model file, or click the button to browse to and select a model file.

If the model file you select contains separate sections, such as .LIB sections in PrimeSim HSPICE, the sections are listed in a menu in the Section column for that row.

4. Ensure the check box in the En column is clicked for model files you want to enable. Uncheck the check boxes next to any model files you want to disable.
5. If the model file you choose contains sections, choose a section you want to use in the menu that appears in the Section column.

<!-- image -->

If multiple sections exist that need to be included in a single file, you need to include the file multiple times.

6. (Optional) Click the Add Protect Statement check box to add the protect statement to your model file.

This option is enabled by default.

7. Add any additional model files as necessary.

Your model files are now set up.

## Adding CS Include Files

To add CS include files:

1. Click Model and Include Files in the Navigation panel.

The Model and Include files tab page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

2. Click the Include Files tab.

The Model Files tab page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

3. Double-click the "Click to add" text, and either enter the path to an include file, or click the button to browse to and select an include file.
4. Ensure the check box in the En column is clicked for include files you want to enable.

Uncheck the check boxes next to any include files you want to disable.

5. (Optional) Click the Expand Include Files check box to expand the include files.

6. Add any additional include files as necessary.

Your include files are now set up.

## Adding CS VEC Files

To add CS vector files:

1. Click Model and Include Files in the Navigation panel.

The Model and Include files tab page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

2. Click the VEC Files tab.

The VEC Files tab page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

3. Double-click the "Click to add" text, and either enter the path to a vector file, or click the button to browse to and select a vector file.
4. Ensure the check box in the En column is clicked for vector files you want to enable. Uncheck the check boxes next to any vector files you want to disable.
5. Add any additional vector files as necessary.

Your vector file setup is complete.

## Adding CS Design Variables

To add CS design variables:

1. Click Design Variables in the Navigation panel.

The Design Variables page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Double-click the "Click to add" text, and enter the name of a design variable.
3. Double-click in the Value cell next to the design variable name you create, and enter a value for the design variable.
4. Ensure the check box in the En column is clicked for model files you want to enable. Uncheck the check boxes next to any model files you want to disable.

## Adding CS Analyses

To add CS analyses:

1. Click Analyses in the Navigation panel.

The Analyses page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Click the check box next to each analysis you want to include in your simulation setup.

The Tran and Stateye analyses are selected by default.

## Note:

WaveView supports only TRAN section of the PSF-XL format for corners, MC, and sweeps. For details, see SolvNetPlus article 000040866, 'PSFXL Format Support in WaveView'.

3. Click Add to add the selected analyses.

The selected analyses are displayed in the Navigation panel.

4. Click the name of an analysis in the Navigation panel.

The analysis setup details are displayed in the Setup panel. For information on analysis setup details, see the HSPICE Reference Manual: Commands and Control Options .

5. Once all analyses are set up, click the check box next to each analysis name in the Navigation panel to enable it.

## Adding CS Sweep Data

## Note:

By default, all added sweeps are added to the default dataname Sweep Group. To create a new sweep group, see Creating New CS Sweep Groups.

To add CS sweep data:

1. Click Sweep Data in the Navigation panel.

The Sweep Data page is displayed.

<!-- image -->

2. Double-click the "Add Variable" text, and choose a design variable you already have as part of your simulation setup from the menu that opens.

The value for the selected design variable appears in the nominal column.

3. Double-click in the Values column next to the design variable name you select, and enter one or more values for additional sweeps separated by commands.

New sweeps are automatically created in new columns.

4. Double-click the "Click to add" column heading to add additional sweeps.

A new column is created with the Sweep &lt;n&gt; heading for each new sweep.

5. Double-click a table cell in the Sweep &lt;n&gt; column for that sweep, and enter a value.
6. Create any additional sweeps as needed, then ensure the check box in the column heading for each sweep name is selected for each sweep you want to enable.

All created sweeps are enabled by default.

Your sweeps are now set up.

- Creating New CS Sweep Groups

## Creating New CS Sweep Groups

To create a new sweep group:

## Generating CS Sweeps

To generate a sweep:

1. Click the Generate Sweeps button on the Sweep Data setup page.

The Generate Sweeps dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

## Adding CS Probes

To add a probe:

1. Click the Probe and Equations category in the Navigation panel. The Probe and Equations page opens with either the Probe tab page or Equation tab page visible.
2. Click the Probe tab.

The Probe tab page opens.

<!-- image -->

3. Click the Click to add text in the probes table. A text box appears in the table, and the Type and Variable text boxes appear as well.
4. Choose a probe type from the Type menu.
5. Enter a variable name in the Variable text box (or Variable 1 if you select Differential Voltage as the probe type), or click the button to select an object from the CS Connection View.
6. If you select Differential Voltage , enter a second variable name in the Variable 2 text box, or click the button to select an object from the CS Connection View.
7. Enter a signal name to probe, and click Enter . If the signal can be probed, the signal name is added to the table
8. (Optional) Click the check box in the Plot column to plot results for a probe. The signal is plotted on completion of a successful simulation run.
9. (Optional) Use Plot Type to set one or multiple plot types with different analysis types. When one probe has multiple analysis types, the plot type setting field shows available

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

analysis types as check boxes. Different plot types are displayed under different waveform tab titles when plotted.

10. Click Apply to save your changes.

<!-- image -->

## Saving and Loading Probe Measure Files

To save a probe measure file, click the Save button in the lower right-hand corner of the Probe tab (accessible from the Probe &amp; Equation tab in the Channel Simulation and Analysis window). The probe measure file is saved.

To load a probe measure file, click the Load button in the lower right-hand corner of the Probe tab (accessible from the Probe &amp; Equation tab in the Channel Simulation and Analysis window). The probe measure file is loaded.

## Removing Probes

To remove a probe:

1. Ensure the Probe tab page is open (accessible from the Probe &amp; Equation tab in the Channel Simulation and Analysis window).
2. Click the button at the end of the table row for the probe you want to remove.

## Note:

If you accidentally delete one or more probes, click Reset in the lower righthand corner to restore all probes setup to the previously saved version.

3. Click Apply to save your changes.

## Enabling and Disabling Probes

To enable a probe in your setup (accessible from the Probe tab page on the Probe &amp; Equation tab), click the check box next to a probe name, and click Apply .

To disable a probe, uncheck the check box to the left of a probe name, and click Apply . Any disabled probes are not included as part of your design when it is simulated.

## Loading Probes

To load a probe measure file, click Load on the Probe tab page (accessible from the Probe &amp; Equation tab).

## Saving Probes

To save a probe measure file, click Save on the on the Probe tab page (accessible from the Probe &amp; Equation tab).

## Adding CS Equations

To add an equation:

1. Click the Probe and Equations category in the Navigation panel.

The Probe and Equations page opens with either the Probe tab page or Equation tab page visible.

<!-- image -->

## 2. Click the Equation tab.

The Equation tab page opens.

<!-- image -->

3. Click Click to add in the Equation column, and enter a signal (or expression) directly into the text box that appears, or create an equation from the calculator that opens.

The function is added to your equation. Moving your pointer over any of the functions gives you descriptions of the function arguments.

4. Enter a name in the Name column for the equation you create.

For more information on the calculator and calculator functions, see Working With the Equation Builder.

## SPUTIL

The S-parameter Manipulation Utility (SPUTIL) is a standalone executable, which gives you access to the PrimeSim HSPICE S-element features without invoking a PrimeSim HSPICE simulation or additional utility functions. You can also use the tool to predict and verify the behavior of given S-parameters in advance of PrimeSim HSPICE simulation runs.

To open this utility, click SPUTIL in the Utilities section of the Waveform tab.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The S-Parameter Manipulation Utility window opens. The Runset pane is where you set S-parameter commands, and the Result pane is for checking output results after running the SPUTIL.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Adding and Editing S-Parameter Commands
- Working With Runsets
- Setting S-Parameter Simulation Options
- Running and Stopping S-Parameter Simulations
- Saving and Loading SPUTIL Files
- Working With Results

## Adding and Editing S-Parameter Commands

## Note:

If you want to rename the Default runset after you add commands, see Renaming Runsets for more information.

To add an S-parameter command, choose a command from the Command menu, (which is at the right-hand side of the Runset pane, then click the double arrow button .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The commands you add to your script in the Runset text box is known as a "runset." You can edit your script as necessary in the Runset text box.

See the HSPICE ® User Guide: Signal Integrity Modeling and Analysis for more information on S-parameter commands and command options.

## Working With Runsets

A runset contains all the S-parameter commands and setup for an S-parameter simulation.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Creating and Deleting Runsets
- Renaming Runsets
- Predefining Runsets in the WaveView Initialization File

## Creating and Deleting Runsets

To create a new runset, ensure the S-Parameter Manipulation Tool window is open (click SPUTIL in the Utilities section of the Waveform tab), then click the Add button in the button toolbar. New runsets are added to the Runset menu.

<!-- image -->

To delete a runset, choose a runset from the Runset menu. Then, choose Runset &gt; Delete from the S-Parameter Manipulation Utility window menu bar or click the Delete button in the button toolbar. Deleted runsets are removed from the Runset menu.

## Renaming Runsets

To rename a runset:

1. Ensure the S-Parameter Manipulation Tool window is open (click SPUTIL in the Utilities section of the Waveform tab).
2. Choose a runset from the Runset menu that you want to rename.
3. Choose Runset &gt; Rename from the S-Parameter Manipulation Utility window menu bar or click the Rename button in the button toolbar.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The Rename Runset dialog box opens.

4. Enter a new name, and click OK to save your changes.

The runset name is updated in the Runset menu.

## Predefining Runsets in the WaveView Initialization File

You can predefine which runsets you want to automatically load each time you open the SPUTIL.

To define a runset in your .cxinit file, open the .cxinit file, and add a definition for a runset using the following syntax:

```
si_load_spumacro {"runset_name" "SPU_file_path"} For example, to define a runset named ct2 , which is in the /remote/sputil/ct2.spu location, add the following line to your .cxinit file: si_load_spumacro {"c2t" "/remote/sputil/c2t.spu"}
```

Add runset multiple definitions for additional runsets you want to predefine.

## Setting S-Parameter Simulation Options

To set S-parameter simulation options, choose Run &gt; Options from the S-Parameter Manipulation Utility window menu bar.

The SPutil Run Options dialog box opens with the following options:

- Executable text box

This option defines the full path of the sputil executable, which is located from the environment settings.

- Run Directory text box

The option defines where the input file ( *.spu ) and output log file ( *.lis ) is generated. The default directory is $WorkingDir/sputil .

## Running and Stopping S-Parameter Simulations

To run an S-parameter simulation, choose Run &gt; Run from the S-Parameter

Manipulation Utility window menu bar, or click the Run button in the button toolbar. If the simulation is successful, the results are displayed in the Result pane.

To stop an S-parameter simulation, choose Run &gt; Stop from the S-Parameter

Manipulation Utility window menu bar, or click the Stop button in the button toolbar.

<!-- image -->

## Saving and Loading SPUTIL Files

To save an S-Parameter Manipulation Utility file, which contains all the setup information for an S-parameter simulation, choose File &gt; Save from the S-Parameter Manipulation Utility window menu bar. SPUTIL files are saved with the *.spu file extension.

To load an S-Parameter Manipulation Utility file, choose File &gt; Load from the SParameter Manipulation Utility window menu bar.

## Working With Results

Once you complete a successful S-parameter simulation, you can view and apply the results to your simulation.

This section contains information on the following topics:

- Viewing S-Parameter Simulation Results
- Viewing the Output Model File
- Applying Output Model Files to Stages

## Viewing S-Parameter Simulation Results

The results from a successful S-parameter simulation are displayed in the Result pane text box of the S-Parameter Manipulation Utility window.

<!-- image -->

The Result List menu contains a list of runset simulations that are complete. Choose a runset to display its results. You can also view its output model file or apply its model file to a simulation stage.

## Viewing the Output Model File

Once a successful simulation is complete, you can view the output model file in the WaveView tool or a file editor.

Open Output Model With: WaveView FileEditor

Open

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

To view the output model file from a Touchstone file in the WaveView tool, click WaveView , and then click Open . The WaveView tool opens with your output model file loaded.

To view the output model file in a file editor, click File Editor , and then click Open . The File Editor window opens with your output model file loaded. You can edit this file as necessary and save its contents to a file by clicking the Save to File button.

<!-- image -->

## Applying Output Model Files to Stages

To apply an output model file to an S-parameter stage after a successful simulation, choose a stage from the Apply Output Model to Stage menu, and click Apply .

The testbench stage is displayed with the output model file as part of the stage, and the stage Type is changed to S Parameter .

## Run

Once you have your CS testbench, simulation, and probes/equations setup, you can run a simulation. To run a simulation, click the Run button in the Simulation section of the CSA tab.

The simulation is run with the Channel Simulation Job settings that are currently set. See Job Control for more information on changing these job control settings.

## Job Control

To change the channel simulation job control options:

<!-- image -->

1. Click Job Control from the Simulation section of the CSA tab, or click the Job Control button in the button icon menu bar.

The Simulation Job Control window opens.

2. (Optional) Enter a name for your simulation run in the Run Name text field.

The Simulation name is used by default.

3. (Optional) Click Browse to choose a Run Directory.

You can also enter a run directory name in the Run Directory text field. The cx\_simulation directory is created for you by default.

4. In the Test List table, enable or disable any corners you want to include in or exclude from your simulation.
5. (Optional) Click Run Options to specify where to run the simulations and how many simulations to run in parallel.
3. See Setting Run Options for more information on setting run options.
6. Click Start to run the simulations.

As the simulation runs, the status is displayed in the Log tab page. Any errors that occur are also displayed here.

Click the Stop All button if you need to abort a simulation while it is running.

## Setting Run Options

The job control Run Options specify where to run your simulations (local or remote server) and how many parallel simulations to run. By default, simulations are run on a local server, and two jobs are run in parallel.

To set the simulation run options:

1. Click the Run Options button, which is located in the Simulation Job Control window (click Job Control from the Simulation section on the CSA tab).

The Run Options window opens.

2. Click the Job Distribution tab.

The Job Distribution tab page is displayed.

3. If you want to run simulations locally, click Local Server .

<!-- image -->

Otherwise, skip to Step 5.

4. Enter a the number of simulation jobs you want to run in parallel.

By default, two simulation jobs are run in parallel. Skip to step Step 11.

5. Click Remote Server to run your simulation jobs on a remote server.
6. Choose the type of network on which the jobs are run: GRID , LSF , or Other .
7. Enter any options you want include when running jobs.
8. Enter the number of jobs to run in parallel on the remote server.

Three simulation jobs are run in parallel by default.

9. Click the Result Handling tab.

The Result Handling tab page is displayed.

10. Enable or disable the results handling options, as well as how you want signals plotted after a simulation is complete.

## Note:

If you enable the Result History option, a date and time stamp is appended to any additional results that come before the current results. For example:

```
Simulation.1-Dec04-1157.tr0 (1st run result) Simulation.2-Dec04-1200.tr0 (2nd run result) Simulation.tr0 (current result)
```

11. Click OK to save your changes.

## Customizing the WaveView Tool

## Setting Key Bindings (Shortcut Keys)

To open the shortcut key settings, click Settings on the Waveform tab, and choose Key Bindings from the menu that opens. The BindKey Setting Finder window opens.

This section describes the following topics:

- Customizing Shortcut Keys
- Top Menu-Operated Shortcut Key Functions
- WaveView Toolbar Shortcut Key Functions
- Other Shortcut Key Functions

## Customizing Shortcut Keys

Shortcut key settings can be customized for key action in the WaveView windows.

The following shortcut keys are allowed:

- A to Z
- 0 - 9
- Ctrl+A to Ctrl+Z
- Ctrl+0 to Ctrl+9

<!-- image -->

- Shift
- Esc
- Delete
- Backspace
- Up Arrow
- Down Arrow

Except for the five function keys (Eec, Delete, Backspace, Up, and Down), a key-down action and a key-up action can be associated with each key.

The available actions can be categorized into the following types:

- menuFunctionName: Equivalent to the top menu actions.
- wctrlFunctionName: Equivalent to the waveview control button actions.
- wcmdFunctionName: Special waveview command actions.

The Bind-Key dialog box automatically flags warnings if the selected action is not allowed for a key event. Select your auto-repeat and action preferences and click Apply to apply the change or click Save to apply and save the change.

## Reading the Key Binding File

The key binding file must be named .spxkey . The WaveView tool can read this file from these different locations, with the following precedence:

- User-specified file name
- -spxkey option usage
- current\_working\_directory/.spxkey
- $(SX\_HOME)/.spxkey (if SX\_HOME is defined)
- $(HOME)/.spxkey (if HOME is defined)

The WaveView tool can also read the .sae.spxkey file with the following precedence:

- $(SX\_HOME)/sae.spxkey (if SX\_HOME is defined)
- $(HOME)/sae.spxkey (if HOME is defined)

SX\_HOME is a user-defined environment variable; HOME is a shell variable which defaults to a user's home directory.

Settings read first are overridden by those read later in the sequence.

<!-- image -->

wcmdJumpCursorBackwardwcmdJumpCursorForward wcmdResetZoom wcmdUndoZoom wcmdRedoZoom

These functions are duplicates of the same 'menu' shortcut key functions. They are supported only for backward compatibility.

wcmdToggleLayoutMode

Switches between Stack and Row/Column layout modes.

wcmdSigAdd wcmdSigDiff wcmdSigMultiply wcmdSigDivide

Performs Add (+), Differential (-), Multiply (* - represented as Shift+8 under KEY in the BindKey Settings Finder), and Divide (/) operations on selected single or multiple signals.

Behavior of operations is as follows:

- When a single signal is selected:
- Add , Multiply - show the original signal.
- Differential - show the data of -signal .
- Divide - show the data of /signal .

<!-- image -->

- When multiple signals are selected:
- Add - add the signals (order of signals does not matter).
- Multiply - multiply the signals (order of signals does not matter).
- Differential - perform the operation on selected signals in the order topto-down as they appear in the Signal List.
- Divide - perform the operation on selected signals in the order top-todown as they appear in the Signal List.

For example, selecting v(0) and v(out) and selecting Differential (or the shortcut key -) calculates the differential operation "v(0) - v(out)".

## Saving Preference Files

To save preferences into a file:

1. Ensure the Preference Settings window is open (click Preferences on the Configuration tab).
2. Click the Apply-Save button.

The Preference Save Location dialog box opens.

3. Choose a location, either in your home directory, the working directory, or in a path you enter by typing or choosing from the file browser.

## Note:

Select Save as PrimeWave Design Environment Preference Name to save the preference settings in PrimeWave preference format.

For example, if you have Number of Significant Digits set to 13 in the Preference Settings window, this will be saved as precision\_digits 5 by default, but if you select Save as PrimeWave Design Environment Preference Name , it will be saved as wfWVPrecisionDigits 5.

4. Click OK to save the file.

## Loading Preference Files

To load an existing preference file:

1. Ensure the Preference Settings window is open (click Preferences on the Configuration tab).
2. Click the Load button.

The Load Preference File dialog box opens.

3. Browse to and select your preference file, and then click OK .

## Note:

The WaveView tool can read WaveView-related preferences from the synopsys\_custom.spxrc file.

## Mapping Bus Values

To open a bus mnemonic map file, click Settings on the Waveform tab, and choose Bus Mnemonic Map from the menu that opens.

Bus values can be mapped to predefined text strings. You can provide a translation table in an external file using the following syntax:

## Syntax

```
# comment lines start with '#' value1 name1 value2 name2 …
```

The values are the bus values to be mapped.

The following formats are supported:

- 2400
- 0xAF32
- 'hAF32
- 'b1001\_0100\_0101
- 'd2400

<!-- image -->

- 'b110110111100
- 'o371

The names are mapped to text strings. A text string must be quoted if the name contains spaces.

Wildcards are supported in Bus Mnemonic expressions. The ? character is a single bit for wildcards. It works only on 'b, 'o, and 'h.

## For example:

2'b1?

4'h1?1?

3'o1?1

<!-- image -->

## Linux Platforms

The following troubleshooting categories are available for Linux platforms:

## Screen Refresh

When running in Linux 7.0 or later, waveview screen content is not refreshed after being blocked by other windows.

The problem is related to the backing store setting of your X server. Waveview windows in the WaveView tool rely on the backing store function of X server to refresh screen content.

You have two options to solve this problem: Turn on the backing store setting of your Xwindow server, or turn on the Internal Screen Refresh option in the Preference Settings.

To check the backing store setting of your X server, run the following:

xdpyinfo If the following output appears, the backing store function of your X server is turned off:

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

```
options: backing-store NO, save-unders NO
```

Enable backing store of your X server by inserting the following line in the Screen section of your X server configuration file (normally /etc/X11/XF86Config or /etc/X11/ XF86Config-4 , but backing\_store also works):

```
Option "backingstore"
```

Alternatively, you can run your X server with the option +bs to obtain the same result without editing your configuration file. Restart your X server, then run the xdpyinfo command again to verify that backing store is enabled. Recent Red Hat Linux distributions (7.0 and 7.1) include XFree86 4.x binaries with backing store disabled by default.

The backingstore option might not work properly if overlay mode is enabled.

## Alternative Methods for Backingstore Setup

To change the backingstore attribute, you must have root privileges.

## Locate the XServers File

This file can be in a variety of locations. Most Linux distributions place the file in /etc/X11/ xdm/Xservers. You might have to look around for your Xserver configuration files.

## Enable Backing-store for Your Xserver

The following example is of a /var/X11/xdm/Xservers file:

```
:0 /usr/bin/X11/X +bs
```

The +bs server command-line option turns on the backing store.

## Restart Your Xserver to Enable the Changes

This varies system to system, but usually logging out and back in again makes the program that starts the Xserver read in the Xservers file again. On Linux you can also restart the Xserver by pressing Control + Alt + Backspace

## With GNOME

If you are using GNOME, modify /etc/X11/gdm/gdm.conf and change the following lines from:

[servers]

0=/usr/bin/X11/X

```
to [servers] 0=/usr/bin/X11/X +bs
```

Then, restart your Xserver.

## Program Fails During Startup on Linux Platforms

This problem might happen if the executable and Linux OS version are not compatible. The fail occurs in the license initialization code used by the Flexlm license manager. Linux is known to have a wide range of kernel variations; fails might occur if the system calls in the kernel are not compatible with the system calls required by the license manager code.

The current release includes binary for Linux 6, 7, and 8 OS. Lower OS executable might fail on a higher OS. For example, the Linux 6 binary might fail on Linux 7/8. Make sure that you select a proper executable for your specific Linux OS.

## X-Window Font Warnings

When the WaveView tool is started on a remote host and displayed on a local X-Windows server, the application might start with some Motif Font warning messages if the default character set cannot be found on the local display. The following warning messages are typical:

- Warning: Missing charsets in String to FontSet conversion
- Warning: Cannot convert string "-dt-interface system-medium-r-normal-l*-*-*-*-*-*-*-*-*" to type FontSet
- Warning: Missing charsets in String to FontSet conversion
- Warning: Unable to load any usable fontset
- Warning:

Name: FONTLIST\_DEFAULT\_TAG\_STRING

Class: XmRendition

Conversion failed. Cannot load font.

- Warning:

Name: FONTLIST\_DEFAULT\_TAG\_STRING

<!-- image -->

Class: XmRendition

Conversion failed. Cannot load font.

As a result, text messages in some of the dialog boxes might disappear. To solve this problem, follow these steps to modify the X font resource settings.

1. Save the X setting by running:
2. Edit file "xrdb\_org" to change the values of the following resources to use "fixed" (or 9x15) as the default font:
3. After editing, run the following line to apply the change to your local X-Windows server:

```
xrdb -query > xrdb_org
```

```
*FontList: fixed *buttonFontList: fixed *labelFontList: fixed *textFontList: fixed
```

```
xrdb -load xrdb_org
```

## XmTextField Font Warning

Symptom: Cannot type text in "text field" entry in dialog boxes.

This problem is a Motif X-Server problem. The following warning message is issued in a non-English X-Windows environment:

## Warning:

```
Name: td_text Class: XmTextField Character '\123' not supported in font. Discarded.
```

This warning message is usually issued multiple times when the file loading dialog box (or any other dialog box with a text field) is open. In the case of the file loading dialog box, file name text string is not automatically filled into the File Name field when a file entry is selected.

To solve this problem, the following Linux environment variables need to be set:

```
setenv LANG C (or setenv LANG en_US.iso88591) setenv LC_CTYPE C
```

<!-- image -->

## Cannot Change Flexlm License File

The Flexlm license manager stores the location of the license file after the application successfully starts. The stored license file is used as the default license file the next time the application starts.

The stored setting needs to be removed when installing a new license file to a different location.

To remove the default setting on Linux, edit the file .flexlmrc in your home directory to remove the line starting with SANDWORK\_LICENSE\_FILE.

To remove the default setting on Windows, click the Start button, choose Run , and enter regedit to edit the Windows Registry. Browse to HKEY\_LOCAL\_MACHINE &gt; SOFTWARE &gt; FLEXlm License Manager and delete the SANDWORK\_LICENSE\_FILE entry.

<!-- image -->
